Test Case 4: How to setup cascading replication

Logical cascading replication

Database A -> Primary Database (Publisher)

Database B -> Intermediate Subscriber, publisher Database A

Database C -> Final Subscriber, publisher Database B

Step 1: We have two subscriber standby1 and standby2

Standby 1 is subscriber for primary and standby 2 is subscriber for standby 1

make change in standby1

Modify the following parameters in postgresql.conf file

Listen_address='*'

Wal_level=logical

Port=5432

Step 2: Modify pg_hba.conf file and add the publication/subscription node ipaddress

host all logstd 192.168.1.8/32 md4 ---destination

host all logstd 192.168.1.9/32 md4 ---source

Step 3: Restart postgresql on standby

pg_ctl stop

pg_ctl start

Step 4: create user in standby1

Create user logstd superuser encrypted password 'abc';

Step 5: Create publication and add table to it.

Create publication mystd1;

Alter publication mystd1 add table reptab2;

Step 6: On Standby2 create a database stdtarget

create database targetdb2;

Note: logical replication can also work for different database from different PostgreSQL server even on different architecture

It also works within in same PostgreSQL server with different database

Step 7: Connect to stdtarget and create the table structure of reptab2.

create table reptab2(deptno int primary key,deptname varchar(20),city varchar(20),deptbuld varchar(20));

Step 8: Create subscription from standby1 to standby

Create subscription mysub2 connection 'host=192.168.1.8 dbname=targetdb user=logstd password=abc' publication mystd1;

Step 9: Check on standby 1

select * from pg_replication_slots;

\dRp

Select * from pg_stat_replication

Step 10: Insert row in primary and check whether it is replicated in standby1 and standby1.

insert into reptab2 values(3,'IT',Montreal','ITBULD');

Select * from reptab2;

Steps:

  1. Drop table and subscription.

drop table reptab2;

in standby1

Server Parameters Tuning

docs.title: Introduction to Server Parameters
docs.text:
• Parameter tuning is a process.
  • Server configuration parameters affect the behavior of the database system.
  • 'Out of Box' settings are not suitable for all environments.
  • Not all systems are designed the same.
  • User interaction with the parameters can be segregated as:

Via Configuration File

Via SQL

Via the Shell

Memory Parameters: Shared Buffers

  • Shared Buffers is the amount of ram that can be allocated to shared buffers.
  • Ideally contains pages being modified or read
  • Shared Buffers uses LRU algorithm to flush the pages from this area.
  • Pg_buffercache extension shows what is inside shared_buffers.
  • Pg_stat_statements show the block hit and read for each sql.
  • pg_statio_user_tables and pg_statio_user_indexes views to see what is in the cache.

Work Mem

  • Work Mem is used for Complex Sorting or hash tables.
  • In-memory sorts are much faster than sorts spilling to disk.
  • Default Value is 4MB.
  • Memory allocated for each sort operations (ORDER BY, DISTINCT) and merge joins
  • Setting this parameter globally can cause very high memory usage as this parameter is used by per user sort operation.
  • Work Mem * Total Sort Operations for all sort operations

Maintenance_Work_mem

  • Maintenance_work_mem is a memory setting used for maintenance tasks.
  • Default value is 64MB.
  • Setting a large value helps in tasks like:

VACUUM

RESTORE

CREATE INDEX

ADD FOREIGN KEY

ALTER TABLE.

Wal_Buffers

  • The amount of shared memory used for WAL data that has not yet been written to disk.
  • PostgreSQL writes its WAL (write ahead log) record into the buffers and then these buffers are flushed to disk.
  • The contents of the WAL buffers are written out to disk at every transaction commit,
  • Default Size is 16MB.
  • Higher value is ideal for concurrent connections.

Effective_Cache_Size

  • Effective_cache_size provides an estimate of the memory available for disk caching.
  • It is just an estimate; no exact actual memory is allocated.
  • It instructs the optimizer the amount of cache available in the kernel.
  • Lower value will discourage the query planner to use indexes, even if they are helpful.
  • Default value is 4GB.
  • lower value prefers sequence scans over index scans.

Checkpoint_timeout

  • Maximum time between automatic WAL checkpoints, in seconds
  • Default value is 5 Minutes.
  • Increasing this parameter can increase the amount of time needed for crash recovery.
  • Frequent check pointing results in continuous writes to disk.
  • More volume of data written to wal logs when checkpoint interval are less.
  • Shutdown may take more time when this value is increased.

Daily Monitoring, Performance & Maintenance Queries

docs.title: Server Start Time / Uptime

SELECT date_trunc('second', current_timestamp - pg_postmaster_start_time()) AS "Uptime"

docs.title: Database Count (Total & Prod)
docs.text:
WITH db_counts AS (

SELECT

COUNT(*) AS "TOTAL_DB",

SUM(CASE WHEN datname ILIKE '%prod%' AND datname NOT LIKE 'ZZZ%' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS "PROD_DB"

FROM pg_database

WHERE datistemplate = false

AND datname NOT ILIKE 'ZZZ%'

AND datname NOT ILIKE '%prodx'

)

SELECT * FROM db_counts;

docs.title: Total Cluster Size
docs.text:
SELECT

SUM(size_gb) AS "Total Size (GB)"

FROM

(SELECT

pg_database.datname AS database,

pg_database_size(pg_database.datname) / (1024.0 * 1024 * 1024) AS size_gb

FROM pg_database

WHERE datistemplate = false

AND pg_database_size(pg_database.datname) > 0) AS subquery;

docs.text:
SELECT

pg_database.datname AS database,

pg_size_pretty(pg_database_size(pg_database.datname)) AS size

FROM pg_database

WHERE datistemplate = false

AND pg_database_size(pg_database.datname) > 0

count(*) AS used_connections

COALESCE(state, 'background') AS state,

COUNT(*)

GROUP BY state

WHERE name IN (

docs.title: Long Running Sessions (> 1 minute)
docs.text:
SELECT pid, usename, datname, application_name, now() - xact_start AS duration, query_id, query

FROM pg_stat_activity

WHERE pid <> pg_backend_pid()

AND state IN ('idle in transaction', 'active')

AND now() - xact_start > INTERVAL '1 minute'

ORDER BY duration DESC;

docs.title: Long Running Queries [os-stats/extensions]
docs.text:
WITH srv AS (
    SELECT
        (SELECT count(*) FROM regexp_matches(pg_read_file('/proc/cpuinfo',0,4194304,true),'^processor','gn'))::numeric AS vcpus,
        (regexp_match(pg_read_file('/proc/meminfo',0,65536,true),'MemTotal:\s+(\d+)'))[1]::numeric / 1024           AS ram_mb,
        -- CLK_TCK detected from my own backend: start time in ticks (stat field 22) / start time in seconds since boot
        (SELECT round( (string_to_array(regexp_replace(pg_read_file('/proc/'||pg_backend_pid()||'/stat',0,4096,true), '^.*\) ', ''), ' '))[20]::numeric
                     / ( EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM a.backend_start)
                       - (EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM clock_timestamp()) - split_part(pg_read_file('/proc/uptime',0,256,true),' ',1)::numeric) )
                     / 10 ) * 10
         FROM pg_stat_activity a WHERE a.pid = pg_backend_pid())                                                   AS clk_tck
),
tmp AS (                     -- temp files in use right now
    SELECT (regexp_match(name, '^pgsql_tmp(\d+)\.'))[1]::int AS pid, count(*) AS temp_files, sum(size) AS temp_bytes
    FROM pg_ls_tmpdir() GROUP BY 1
),
lk AS (                      -- locks held / waiting
    SELECT pid, count(*) FILTER (WHERE granted) AS locks_held, count(*) FILTER (WHERE NOT granted) AS locks_waiting
    FROM pg_locks GROUP BY pid
),
blk AS (                     -- how many sessions each pid is blocking
    SELECT b.pid, count(*) AS blocks_count
    FROM pg_stat_activity x CROSS JOIN LATERAL unnest(pg_blocking_pids(x.pid)) AS b(pid)
    GROUP BY b.pid
),
raw AS (                     -- read /proc for each session; a vanished process just gives NULLs
    SELECT a.*,
           pg_read_file('/proc/'||a.pid||'/stat',   0, 4096,  true) AS stat_txt,
           pg_read_file('/proc/'||a.pid||'/status', 0, 65536, true) AS status_txt,
           pg_read_file('/proc/'||a.pid||'/io',     0, 4096,  true) AS io_txt
    FROM pg_stat_activity a
    WHERE a.state <> 'idle' AND a.pid <> pg_backend_pid()
),
s AS (
    SELECT r.*,
           f[1]                                                          AS os_state,     -- R running, S sleeping, D disk wait
           (f[12]::numeric + f[13]::numeric) / srv.clk_tck               AS cpu_sec,      -- utime + stime (stat fields 14, 15)
           f[37]                                                         AS processor,    -- last core (stat field 39)
           COALESCE((regexp_match(r.status_txt,'RssAnon:\s+(\d+)'))[1]::numeric, 0)  / 1024 AS private_mb,
           COALESCE((regexp_match(r.status_txt,'RssShmem:\s+(\d+)'))[1]::numeric, 0) / 1024 AS shared_mb,
           COALESCE((regexp_match(r.io_txt,'read_bytes:\s+(\d+)'))[1]::numeric, 0)          AS read_bytes,
           COALESCE((regexp_match(r.io_txt,'write_bytes:\s+(\d+)'))[1]::numeric, 0)         AS write_bytes,
           COALESCE(t.temp_files,0)    AS temp_files,  COALESCE(t.temp_bytes,0)    AS temp_bytes,
           COALESCE(l.locks_held,0)    AS locks_held,  COALESCE(l.locks_waiting,0) AS locks_waiting,
           COALESCE(bk.blocks_count,0) AS blocks_count
    FROM raw r
    CROSS JOIN srv
    CROSS JOIN LATERAL (SELECT string_to_array(regexp_replace(r.stat_txt, '^.*\) ', ''), ' ') AS f) st
    LEFT JOIN tmp t  ON t.pid  = r.pid
    LEFT JOIN lk  l  ON l.pid  = r.pid
    LEFT JOIN blk bk ON bk.pid = r.pid
    WHERE r.stat_txt IS NOT NULL                    -- process ended while we were reading: skip it
)
SELECT
    COALESCE(s.leader_pid, s.pid)                                                        AS session_pid,
    count(*)                                                                             AS processes,
    max(s.usename)                                                                       AS usename,
    max(s.application_name)                                                              AS app,
    max(host(s.client_addr))                                                             AS client,
    max(s.state)  FILTER (WHERE s.leader_pid IS NULL)                                    AS state,
    max(COALESCE(s.wait_event_type||':'||s.wait_event,'on CPU')) FILTER (WHERE s.leader_pid IS NULL) AS wait_event,
    string_agg(DISTINCT s.os_state, ',')                                                 AS os_state,
    date_trunc('second', max(clock_timestamp() - s.query_start))                         AS running_for,
    date_trunc('second', max(clock_timestamp() - s.xact_start))                          AS txn_age,
    -- CPU
    max(srv.vcpus)                                                                       AS server_vcpus,
    round(sum(s.cpu_sec)/GREATEST(EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM clock_timestamp()-min(s.backend_start)),1),2)                 AS cores_used,
    round(sum(s.cpu_sec)/GREATEST(EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM clock_timestamp()-min(s.backend_start)),1)/max(srv.vcpus)*100,1) AS cpu_pct_of_server,
    string_agg(s.processor, ',')                                                         AS cores_now,
    -- MEMORY
    round(sum(s.private_mb))                                                             AS private_mem_mb,
    round(sum(s.private_mb)/max(srv.ram_mb)*100,2)                                       AS mem_pct_of_server,
    round(max(s.shared_mb))                                                              AS shared_buffers_touched_mb,
    -- TEMP (spilled sorts/hashes in use now)
    sum(s.temp_files)                                                                    AS temp_files_now,
    pg_size_pretty(sum(s.temp_bytes)::bigint)                                            AS temp_used_now,
    -- DISK I/O (since connection start)
    pg_size_pretty(sum(s.read_bytes)::bigint)                                            AS disk_read,
    pg_size_pretty(sum(s.write_bytes)::bigint)                                           AS disk_written,
    -- LOCKS / BLOCKING
    sum(s.locks_held)                                                                    AS locks_held,
    sum(s.locks_waiting)                                                                 AS locks_waiting,
    max(array_to_string(pg_blocking_pids(s.pid), ',')) FILTER (WHERE s.leader_pid IS NULL) AS blocked_by,
    sum(s.blocks_count)                                                                  AS sessions_it_blocks,
    -- VACUUM impact
    max(age(s.backend_xmin))                                                             AS xmin_age_txns,
    -- QUERY
    left(max(s.query) FILTER (WHERE s.leader_pid IS NULL), 150)                          AS query
FROM s CROSS JOIN srv
GROUP BY COALESCE(s.leader_pid, s.pid)
ORDER BY cpu_pct_of_server DESC, sum(s.temp_bytes) DESC;

docs.title: Active Connections Excluding Current Query
docs.text:
SELECT age(clock_timestamp(), query_start), usename, datname, query

FROM pg_stat_activity

WHERE state != 'idle'

AND query NOT ILIKE '%pg_stat_activity%'

ORDER BY age DESC;

docs.title: Sessions Waiting on an Event
docs.text:
SELECT usename, datname, query, wait_event_type, wait_event

FROM pg_stat_activity

WHERE state != 'idle'

AND wait_event IS NOT NULL;

docs.title: Session Count by Wait Event Type
docs.text:
SELECT

COALESCE(wait_event_type, 'None') AS wait_type,

COUNT(*) AS session_count

FROM pg_stat_activity

WHERE backend_type = 'client backend'

GROUP BY wait_type;

docs.title: Idle-in-Transaction / Aborted Sessions
docs.text:
SELECT * FROM pg_stat_activity

WHERE state IN ('idle in transaction', 'idle in transaction (aborted)');

docs.title: Ginview Sessions Running > 30 Minutes (per database)
docs.text:
SELECT DISTINCT

current_timestamp AS logdate,

a.pid, a.usename, a.datname, a.application_name,

n.nspname AS schema_name, a.state,

TO_CHAR(now() - a.xact_start, 'HH24:MI') AS duration,

a.query_id,

regexp_replace(a.query, '\\s+', ' ', 'g') AS query

FROM pg_stat_activity a

JOIN pg_locks l ON a.pid = l.pid

JOIN pg_class c ON l.relation = c.oid

JOIN pg_namespace n ON c.relnamespace = n.oid

JOIN pg_database d ON a.datname = d.datname

WHERE a.state = 'active'

AND a.application_name = 'w3wp.exe'

AND a.query_start < NOW() - INTERVAL '30 minutes'

AND a.query LIKE '%ginview.%'

AND a.datname = current_database()

AND n.nspname = 'ginview'

ORDER BY a.query_start;

docs.title: Blocking Sessions - Detailed (lock/relation view)
docs.text:
SELECT

d.datname AS database_name,

a.pid AS blocked_pid,

l.mode AS lock_mode,

l.locktype,

l.relation::regclass AS locked_relation,

bl.pid AS blocking_pid

FROM pg_stat_activity AS a

JOIN pg_locks AS l ON a.pid = l.pid

JOIN pg_locks AS bl ON l.locktype = bl.locktype

AND l.relation = bl.relation AND l.pid != bl.pid

JOIN pg_database AS d ON a.datid = d.oid

WHERE l.mode <> 'AccessShareLock'

AND bl.mode <> 'AccessShareLock'

ORDER BY d.datname, a.pid;

docs.title: Step 1: Identify Blocking Sessions
docs.text:
SELECT pid, usename, state, wait_event, query  
FROM pg_stat_activity  
WHERE pid IN (  
SELECT unnest(pg_blocking_pids(pid))  
FROM pg_stat_activity  
);  
<br/>Step 2: Kill Only Blocking Sessions (Best Practice)  
SELECT pg_terminate_backend(pid)  
FROM pg_stat_activity  
WHERE pid IN (  
SELECT unnest(pg_blocking_pids(pid))  
FROM pg_stat_activity);

docs.title: Waiting Connections Count for a Lock
docs.text: SELECT count(DISTINCT pid) FROM pg_locks WHERE granted = false;

docs.title: Cancel a Running Query (graceful)
docs.text:
SELECT pg_cancel_backend(<pid>);

-- Example: SELECT pg_cancel_backend(27735);

docs.title: Terminate a Specific Session
docs.text: SELECT pg_terminate_backend(<pid>);

docs.title: Kill Only Root Blocking Sessions (Best Practice)
docs.text:
SELECT pg_terminate_backend(pid)

FROM pg_stat_activity

WHERE pid IN (

SELECT unnest(pg_blocking_pids(pid))

FROM pg_stat_activity

);

docs.title: Kill All Idle Sessions
docs.text:
SELECT pg_terminate_backend(pg_stat_activity.pid)

FROM pg_stat_activity

WHERE pid <> pg_backend_pid()

AND state = 'idle';

docs.title: Kill All Idle-in-Transaction Sessions
docs.text:
SELECT pg_terminate_backend(pid)

FROM pg_stat_activity

WHERE datname = '<db_name>'

AND state = 'idle in transaction';

docs.title: Kill Sessions Idle Beyond a Time Threshold
docs.text:
SELECT pg_terminate_backend(pid)

FROM pg_stat_activity

WHERE datname = '<db_name>'

AND pid <> pg_backend_pid()

AND state IN ('idle', 'idle in transaction', 'idle in transaction (aborted)', 'disabled')

AND state_change < current_timestamp - INTERVAL '15 minutes';

docs.title: Kill All Active Connections to a Database
docs.text:
SELECT pg_terminate_backend(pid)

FROM pg_stat_activity

WHERE datname = '<db_name>'

AND leader_pid IS NULL;

docs.title: Kill All Connections to a Database Except Current Session
docs.text:
SELECT pg_terminate_backend(pid)

FROM pg_stat_activity

WHERE datname = '<db_name>'

AND pid != pg_backend_pid()

AND leader_pid IS NULL;

docs.title: Terminate All Connections Across All Databases (Except Current)
docs.text:
SELECT pg_terminate_backend(pid)

FROM pg_stat_activity

WHERE pid != pg_backend_pid()

AND datname IS NOT NULL

AND leader_pid IS NULL;

docs.title: Generate Cancel Statements for Active / Idle-in-Transaction Sessions
docs.text:
SELECT 'SELECT pg_cancel_backend(' || pid || ');'

FROM pg_stat_activity

WHERE pid <> pg_backend_pid()

AND state IN ('idle in transaction', 'active');

docs.title: Cluster-wide Heap Cache Hit Ratio
docs.text:
SELECT

SUM(heap_blks_read) AS "Heap Read",

SUM(heap_blks_hit) AS "Heap Hit",

ROUND((SUM(heap_blks_hit) * 100.0) / NULLIF((SUM(heap_blks_hit) + SUM(heap_blks_read)), 0), 2) AS "Hit Ratio Percentage"

FROM pg_statio_user_tables;

docs.title: Cache Hit Ratio per Database
docs.text:
SELECT datname AS "Database", blks_hit, blks_read,

round(blks_hit / (blks_hit + blks_read + 0.00001) * 100, 2) AS "cache hit ratio"

FROM pg_stat_database

WHERE datname IS NOT NULL

ORDER BY 4 ASC;

docs.title: Index Cache Hit Ratio
docs.text:
SELECT

sum(idx_blks_read) AS idx_read,

sum(idx_blks_hit) AS idx_hit,

(sum(idx_blks_hit) - sum(idx_blks_read)) / sum(idx_blks_hit) AS ratio

FROM pg_statio_user_indexes;

docs.title: Overall Cache Hit Ratio (target > 90%)
docs.text:
SELECT sum(blks_hit) * 100 / sum(blks_hit + blks_read) AS hit_ratio

FROM pg_stat_database;

docs.title: Shared Buffer Usage per Database (block count)
docs.text:
SELECT

CASE WHEN c.reldatabase IS NULL THEN ''

WHEN c.reldatabase = 0 THEN ''

ELSE d.datname END AS database,

count(*) AS cached_blocks

FROM pg_buffercache AS c

LEFT JOIN pg_database AS d ON c.reldatabase = d.oid

GROUP BY d.datname, c.reldatabase

ORDER BY 2 DESC;

docs.title: Shared Buffer Status (dirty / clean / empty, in MB)
docs.text:
SELECT buffer_status, round(sum(count) * 8 / 1024) AS "Size(MB)"

FROM (

SELECT CASE isdirty WHEN true THEN 'dirty' WHEN false THEN 'clean' ELSE 'empty' END AS buffer_status,

count(*) AS count

FROM pg_buffercache

GROUP BY buffer_status

UNION ALL

SELECT * FROM (VALUES ('dirty', 0), ('clean', 0), ('empty', 0)) AS tab2(buffer_status, count)

) tab1

GROUP BY buffer_status;

docs.title: Top Tables Cached in Current Database (by buffer count)
docs.text:
SELECT n.nspname, c.relname, count(*) AS buffers

FROM pg_buffercache b

JOIN pg_class c ON b.relfilenode = pg_relation_filenode(c.oid)

AND b.reldatabase IN (0, (SELECT oid FROM pg_database WHERE datname = current_database()))

JOIN pg_namespace n ON n.oid = c.relnamespace

GROUP BY n.nspname, c.relname

ORDER BY 3 DESC

LIMIT 10;

docs.title: How Much of a Table/Index is Buffered (% of relation & shared_buffers)
docs.text:
SELECT

c.relname,

pg_size_pretty(count(*) * 8192) AS buffered,

round(100.0 * count(*) / (SELECT setting FROM pg_settings WHERE name = 'shared_buffers')::integer, 1) AS buffers_percent,

round(100.0 * count(*) * 8192 / pg_table_size(c.oid), 1) AS percent_of_relation

FROM pg_class c

INNER JOIN pg_buffercache b ON b.relfilenode = c.relfilenode

INNER JOIN pg_database d ON (b.reldatabase = d.oid AND d.datname = current_database())

GROUP BY c.oid, c.relname

ORDER BY 3 DESC

LIMIT 10;

docs.title: Buffer Usage-Count Distribution (hotness of pages)
docs.text:
SELECT usagecount, count(*)

FROM pg_buffercache

GROUP BY usagecount

ORDER BY usagecount;

docs.title: % of Relation Cached and % Hot (usagecount > 3)
docs.text:
SELECT c.relname,

count(*) blocks,

round(100.0 * 8192 * count(*) / pg_table_size(c.oid)) AS "% of rel",

round(100.0 * 8192 * count(*) FILTER (WHERE b.usagecount > 3) / pg_table_size(c.oid)) AS "% hot"

FROM pg_buffercache b

JOIN pg_class c ON pg_relation_filenode(c.oid) = b.relfilenode

WHERE b.reldatabase IN (0, (SELECT oid FROM pg_database WHERE datname = current_database()))

AND b.usagecount IS NOT NULL

GROUP BY c.relname, c.oid

ORDER BY 2 DESC

LIMIT 10;

docs.title: Pre-warm a Table into Shared Buffers (pg_prewarm)
docs.text:
-- Check page count first

SELECT oid::regclass AS tbl, relpages FROM pg_class WHERE relname = '<table_name>';

-- Load table into cache

SELECT * FROM pg_prewarm('<table_name>');

docs.title: Check Blocks of a Specific Table in Buffer Cache
docs.text:
SELECT count(*) FROM pg_buffercache

WHERE relfilenode = pg_relation_filenode('<table_name>'::regclass);

docs.title: Dirty Page / Background Writer Stats
docs.text:
SELECT buffers_clean, maxwritten_clean, buffers_backend_fsync

FROM pg_stat_bgwriter;

-- maxwritten_clean and buffers_backend_fsync should ideally be 0

docs.title: Requested vs Timed Checkpoints (health check)
docs.text:
SELECT 'bad' AS checkpoints

FROM pg_stat_bgwriter

WHERE checkpoints_req > checkpoints_timed;

docs.title: Autovacuum & Track-Counts Enabled?
docs.text: SELECT name, setting FROM pg_settings WHERE name IN ('autovacuum', 'track_counts');

docs.title: Autovacuum-Related Configuration Parameters
docs.text: SELECT * FROM pg_settings WHERE category LIKE 'Autovacuum%';

docs.title: Dead/Live Tuple Counts & Last Vacuum/Analyze Times
docs.text:
SELECT schemaname, relname, n_live_tup, n_dead_tup,

round(n_dead_tup::float / n_live_tup::float * 100) AS dead_pct,

autovacuum_count, last_vacuum, last_analyze, last_autovacuum, last_autoanalyze

FROM pg_stat_all_tables

WHERE n_live_tup > 0

ORDER BY n_dead_tup DESC;

docs.title: Tables With ≥ 50% Dead Tuples (bloat candidates)
docs.text:
SELECT * FROM (

SELECT schemaname, relname, n_live_tup, n_dead_tup,

round(n_dead_tup::float / n_live_tup::float * 100) dead_pct,

autovacuum_count, last_vacuum, last_analyze, last_autovacuum, last_autoanalyze

FROM pg_stat_all_tables

WHERE n_live_tup > 10

ORDER BY n_dead_tup DESC

) sub

WHERE dead_pct >= 50

ORDER BY dead_pct DESC;

docs.title: Tables Currently Qualifying for Autovacuum
docs.text:
SELECT *,

n_dead_tup > av_threshold AS av_needed,

CASE WHEN reltuples > 0 THEN round(100.0 * n_dead_tup / reltuples) ELSE 0 END AS pct_dead

FROM (

SELECT N.nspname, C.relname,

pg_stat_get_tuples_inserted(C.oid) AS n_tup_ins,

pg_stat_get_tuples_updated(C.oid) AS n_tup_upd,

pg_stat_get_tuples_deleted(C.oid) AS n_tup_del,

pg_stat_get_live_tuples(C.oid) AS n_live_tup,

pg_stat_get_dead_tuples(C.oid) AS n_dead_tup,

C.reltuples AS reltuples,

round(current_setting('autovacuum_vacuum_threshold')::INTEGER

\+ current_setting('autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor')::NUMERIC * C.reltuples) AS av_threshold,

date_trunc('minute', greatest(pg_stat_get_last_vacuum_time(C.oid), pg_stat_get_last_autovacuum_time(C.oid))) AS last_vacuum,

date_trunc('minute', greatest(pg_stat_get_last_analyze_time(C.oid), pg_stat_get_last_autoanalyze_time(C.oid))) AS last_analyze

FROM pg_class C

LEFT JOIN pg_namespace N ON (N.oid = C.relnamespace)

WHERE C.relkind IN ('r', 't')

AND N.nspname NOT IN ('pg_catalog', 'information_schema')

AND N.nspname !~ '^pg_toast'

) AS av

ORDER BY av_needed DESC, n_dead_tup DESC;

docs.title: Check Progress of a Running VACUUM
docs.text: SELECT * FROM pg_stat_progress_vacuum;

docs.title: Run VACUUM Manually
docs.text: VACUUM (VERBOSE, ANALYZE);

docs.title: Table-Level Autovacuum Overrides
docs.text: SELECT reloptions FROM pg_class WHERE relname = '<table_name>';

docs.title: Transaction ID Wraparound Monitoring
docs.text:
WITH max_age AS (

SELECT 2000000000 AS max_old_xid, setting AS autovacuum_freeze_max_age

FROM pg_catalog.pg_settings

WHERE name = 'autovacuum_freeze_max_age'

), per_database_stats AS (

SELECT datname, m.max_old_xid::int, m.autovacuum_freeze_max_age::int,

age(d.datfrozenxid) AS oldest_current_xid

FROM pg_catalog.pg_database d

JOIN max_age m ON (true)

WHERE d.datallowconn

)

SELECT max(oldest_current_xid) AS oldest_current_xid,

max(ROUND(100 * (oldest_current_xid / max_old_xid::float))) AS percent_towards_wraparound,

max(ROUND(100 * (oldest_current_xid / autovacuum_freeze_max_age::float))) AS percent_towards_emergency_autovac

FROM per_database_stats;

docs.title: Database Age (Transaction ID Age per Database)
docs.text:
SELECT datname, age(datfrozenxid), current_setting('autovacuum_freeze_max_age')

FROM pg_database

ORDER BY 2 DESC;

docs.title: Object Age per Database (relfrozenxid)
docs.text:
SELECT c.oid::regclass, age(c.relfrozenxid), pg_size_pretty(pg_total_relation_size(c.oid))

FROM pg_class c

JOIN pg_namespace n ON c.relnamespace = n.oid

WHERE relkind IN ('r', 't', 'm')

AND n.nspname NOT IN ('pg_toast')

ORDER BY 2 DESC;

docs.title: Row Insert / Update / Delete Distribution per Table
docs.text:
SELECT relname,

cast(n_tup_ins AS numeric) / (n_tup_ins + n_tup_upd + n_tup_del) AS ins_pct,

cast(n_tup_upd AS numeric) / (n_tup_ins + n_tup_upd + n_tup_del) AS upd_pct,

cast(n_tup_del AS numeric) / (n_tup_ins + n_tup_upd + n_tup_del) AS del_pct

FROM pg_stat_user_tables

ORDER BY relname;

docs.title: HOT Update Percentage per Table (should be close to 100%)
docs.text:
SELECT relname, n_tup_upd, n_tup_hot_upd,

cast(n_tup_hot_upd AS numeric) / n_tup_upd AS hot_pct

FROM pg_stat_user_tables

WHERE n_tup_upd > 0

ORDER BY hot_pct;

docs.title: List All Indexes in a Schema
docs.text:
SELECT tablename AS "TableName", indexname AS "Index Name", indexdef AS "Index script"

FROM pg_indexes

WHERE schemaname = '<schema_name>'

ORDER BY tablename, indexname;

docs.title: Indexes with Primary/Unique Key Flags
docs.text:
SELECT

c.relnamespace::regnamespace AS schema_name,

c.relname AS table_name,

i.indexrelid::regclass AS index_name,

i.indisprimary AS is_pk,

i.indisunique AS is_unique

FROM pg_index i

JOIN pg_class c ON c.oid = i.indrelid

WHERE c.relname = '<table_name>';

docs.title: Get Indexes with Column Names
docs.text:
SELECT t.relname AS table_name, i.relname AS index_name,

string_agg(a.attname, ',') AS column_name

FROM pg_class t, pg_class i, pg_index ix, pg_attribute a

WHERE t.oid = ix.indrelid

AND i.oid = ix.indexrelid

AND a.attrelid = t.oid

AND a.attnum = ANY(ix.indkey)

AND t.relkind = 'r'

AND t.relname NOT LIKE 'pg_%'

GROUP BY t.relname, i.relname

ORDER BY t.relname, i.relname;

docs.title: Unused Indexes (idx_scan = 0)
docs.text: SELECT * FROM pg_stat_all_indexes WHERE idx_scan = 0 AND schemaname = '<schema_name>';

docs.title: Rarely-Used Indexes (idx_scan < 100)
docs.text:
SELECT

relname AS table_name, indexrelname AS index_name,

pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size(indexrelid)) AS index_size,

idx_scan AS index_scan_count

FROM pg_stat_user_indexes

WHERE idx_scan < 100

ORDER BY index_scan_count ASC, pg_relation_size(indexrelid) DESC;

docs.title: Duplicate Indexes
docs.text:
SELECT ni.nspname || '.' || ct.relname AS "table",

ci.relname AS "dup index",

pg_get_indexdef(i.indexrelid) AS "dup index definition",

i.indkey AS "dup index attributes",

cii.relname AS "encompassing index",

pg_get_indexdef(ii.indexrelid) AS "encompassing index definition",

ii.indkey AS "enc index attributes"

FROM pg_index i

JOIN pg_class ct ON i.indrelid = ct.oid

JOIN pg_class ci ON i.indexrelid = ci.oid

JOIN pg_namespace ni ON ci.relnamespace = ni.oid

JOIN pg_index ii ON ii.indrelid = i.indrelid

AND ii.indexrelid != i.indexrelid

AND (array_to_string(ii.indkey, ' ') || ' ') LIKE (array_to_string(i.indkey, ' ') || ' %')

AND (array_to_string(ii.indcollation, ' ') || ' ') LIKE (array_to_string(i.indcollation, ' ') || ' %')

AND (array_to_string(ii.indclass, ' ') || ' ') LIKE (array_to_string(i.indclass, ' ') || ' %')

AND (array_to_string(ii.indoption, ' ') || ' ') LIKE (array_to_string(i.indoption, ' ') || ' %')

AND NOT (ii.indkey::integer\[\] @> ARRAY\[0\])

AND NOT (i.indkey::integer\[\] @> ARRAY\[0\])

AND i.indpred IS NULL AND ii.indpred IS NULL

AND CASE WHEN i.indisunique THEN ii.indisunique

AND array_to_string(ii.indkey, ' ') = array_to_string(i.indkey, ' ') ELSE true END

JOIN pg_class ctii ON ii.indrelid = ctii.oid

JOIN pg_class cii ON ii.indexrelid = cii.oid

WHERE ct.relname NOT LIKE 'pg_%'

AND NOT i.indisprimary

ORDER BY 1, 2, 3;

docs.title: Index Leaf Fragmentation ≥ 40% (Bloat Check)
docs.text:
SELECT * FROM (

SELECT

current_database() AS database_name,

i.indexname, i.tablename,

pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size(c.oid)) AS index_size,

pg_relation_size(c.oid) AS index_size_bytes,

COALESCE(NULLIF((SELECT avg_leaf_density FROM pgstatindex(c.oid)), 'NaN'::float), 0) AS avg_leaf_density,

COALESCE(NULLIF((SELECT leaf_fragmentation FROM pgstatindex(c.oid)), 'NaN'::float), 0) AS leaf_fragmentation,

COALESCE(s.idx_scan, 0) AS index_scan_count,

'REINDEX INDEX ' || i.indexname || ';' AS statement

FROM pg_indexes i

JOIN pg_class c ON c.relname = i.indexname

JOIN pg_namespace n ON n.oid = c.relnamespace

LEFT JOIN pg_stat_user_indexes s ON s.indexrelid = c.oid

WHERE n.nspname = '<schema_name>'

) sub

WHERE leaf_fragmentation >= 40

AND index_scan_count >= 100

ORDER BY leaf_fragmentation DESC, index_size_bytes DESC;

docs.title: Index Usage % vs Sequential Scans
docs.text:
SELECT relname, 100 * idx_scan / (seq_scan + idx_scan) AS percent_of_times_index_used,

n_live_tup AS rows_in_table

FROM pg_stat_user_tables

WHERE (seq_scan + idx_scan) > 0

ORDER BY n_live_tup DESC;

docs.title: Index Scan % per Table (alternate)
docs.text:
SELECT schemaname, relname, seq_scan, idx_scan,

cast(idx_scan AS numeric) / (idx_scan + seq_scan) AS idx_scan_pct

FROM pg_stat_user_tables

WHERE (idx_scan + seq_scan) > 0

ORDER BY idx_scan_pct;

docs.title: Detect Tables Possibly Missing an Index
docs.text:
SELECT relname, seq_scan - idx_scan AS too_much_seq,

CASE WHEN seq_scan - idx_scan > 0 THEN 'Missing/Ineff Index' ELSE 'OK' END,

pg_relation_size(relname::regclass) AS rel_size, seq_scan, idx_scan

FROM pg_stat_all_tables

WHERE schemaname = '<schema_name>'

AND pg_relation_size(relname::regclass) > 80000

ORDER BY too_much_seq DESC;

docs.title: Average Rows Read per Sequential Scan (potential missing index)
docs.text:
SELECT schemaname, relname, seq_scan, seq_tup_read,

seq_tup_read / seq_scan AS avg, idx_scan

FROM pg_stat_user_tables

WHERE seq_scan > 0

ORDER BY seq_tup_read DESC

LIMIT 25;

docs.title: Average Tuples Read per Index Scan
docs.text:
SELECT indexrelname,

cast(idx_tup_read AS numeric) / idx_scan AS avg_tuples,

idx_scan, idx_tup_read

FROM pg_stat_user_indexes

WHERE idx_scan > 0;

docs.title: How Much Index Data is in Cache
docs.text:
SELECT sum(idx_blks_read) AS idx_read, sum(idx_blks_hit) AS idx_hit

FROM pg_statio_user_indexes;

docs.title: Table Size Excluding Indexes (per database)
docs.text:
SELECT table_name, pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size(quote_ident(table_name))) AS table_size

FROM information_schema.tables

WHERE table_schema NOT IN ('pg_catalog', 'information_schema')

ORDER BY pg_total_relation_size(quote_ident(table_name)) DESC;

docs.title: Table Size Including Indexes (per database)
docs.text:
SELECT table_name, pg_size_pretty(pg_total_relation_size(quote_ident(table_name))) AS table_size

FROM information_schema.tables

WHERE table_schema NOT IN ('pg_catalog', 'information_schema')

ORDER BY pg_total_relation_size(quote_ident(table_name)) DESC;

docs.title: Single Table Size (excl./incl. index)
docs.text:
SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('<schema>.<table>')) AS table_size_excl_index;

SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_total_relation_size('<schema>.<table>')) AS table_size_incl_index;

docs.title: Top Table Sizes with Index Breakdown
docs.text:
SELECT relname,

pg_size_pretty(pg_total_relation_size(relname::regclass)) AS full_size,

pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size(relname::regclass)) AS table_size,

pg_size_pretty(pg_total_relation_size(relname::regclass) - pg_relation_size(relname::regclass)) AS index_size

FROM pg_stat_user_tables

ORDER BY pg_total_relation_size(relname::regclass) DESC

LIMIT 10;

docs.title: Object Sizes with TOAST Info
docs.text:
WITH idx AS (
    SELECT i.indrelid                                   AS table_oid,
           COUNT(*)                                     AS index_count,
           SUM(pg_relation_size(i.indexrelid))          AS index_bytes,
           STRING_AGG(ic.relname || ' (' || pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size(i.indexrelid)) || ')',
                      ', ' ORDER BY pg_relation_size(i.indexrelid) DESC) AS index_list
    FROM   pg_index i
    JOIN   pg_class ic ON ic.oid = i.indexrelid
    GROUP  BY i.indrelid
),
toast AS (
    SELECT t.oid                       AS toast_oid,
           'pg_toast.' || t.relname    AS toast_table,
           'pg_toast.' || ti.relname   AS toast_index
    FROM   pg_class t
    LEFT JOIN pg_index d   ON d.indrelid = t.oid
    LEFT JOIN pg_class ti  ON ti.oid = d.indexrelid
    WHERE  t.relkind = 't'
)
SELECT current_timestamp                                                  AS logdate,
       current_database()                                                 AS "Database",
       n.nspname                                                          AS "Schema",
       c.relname                                                          AS "Object Name",
       CASE c.relkind WHEN 'r' THEN 'table'
                      WHEN 'p' THEN 'partitioned table'
                      WHEN 'm' THEN 'materialized view' END               AS "Object Type",
       ROUND(pg_relation_size(c.oid) / 1048576.0, 2)                      AS "Table Size (MB)",
       tt.toast_table                                                     AS "TOAST Table",
       tt.toast_index                                                     AS "TOAST Index",
       ROUND(COALESCE(pg_total_relation_size(NULLIF(c.reltoastrelid, 0)), 0) / 1048576.0, 2)
                                                                          AS "TOAST Size (MB)",
       ROUND(COALESCE(x.index_bytes, 0) / 1048576.0, 2)                   AS "Index Size (MB)",
       ROUND(pg_total_relation_size(c.oid) / 1048576.0, 2)                AS "Total Size (MB)",
       pg_size_pretty(pg_total_relation_size(c.oid))                      AS "Total Size",
       COALESCE(x.index_count, 0)                                         AS "Index Count",
       x.index_list                                                       AS "Indexes (largest first)"
FROM   pg_class c
JOIN   pg_namespace n ON n.oid = c.relnamespace
LEFT JOIN idx x    ON x.table_oid = c.oid
LEFT JOIN toast tt ON tt.toast_oid = c.reltoastrelid
WHERE  c.relkind IN ('r', 'p', 'm')
AND    n.nspname NOT IN ('pg_catalog', 'information_schema')
AND    n.nspname NOT LIKE 'pg_toast%'
ORDER  BY pg_total_relation_size(c.oid) DESC;

docs.title: Object Size - All Objects, Simplified
docs.text:
SELECT

pg_namespace.nspname AS "Schema", pg_class.relname AS "Object Name",

CASE relkind

WHEN 'r' THEN 'table' WHEN 'i' THEN 'index' WHEN 'S' THEN 'sequence'

WHEN 'v' THEN 'view' WHEN 'm' THEN 'materialized view' WHEN 'c' THEN 'composite type'

WHEN 't' THEN 'TOAST table' WHEN 'f' THEN 'foreign table' ELSE 'other'

END AS "Object Type",

pg_size_pretty(pg_total_relation_size(pg_class.oid)) AS "Total Size"

FROM pg_catalog.pg_class

INNER JOIN pg_catalog.pg_namespace ON pg_class.relnamespace = pg_namespace.oid

WHERE relname NOT LIKE 'pg_%'

AND relkind <> 'd'

ORDER BY pg_total_relation_size(pg_class.oid) DESC;

docs.title: Schema Size (% of Total Database)
docs.text:
SELECT schemaname,

pg_size_pretty(sum(table_size)::bigint) AS schema_size,

(sum(table_size) / pg_database_size(current_database())) * 100 AS percentage_of_total_db

FROM (

SELECT pg_catalog.pg_namespace.nspname AS schemaname,

pg_relation_size(pg_catalog.pg_class.oid) AS table_size

FROM pg_catalog.pg_class

JOIN pg_catalog.pg_namespace ON relnamespace = pg_catalog.pg_namespace.oid

) t

GROUP BY schemaname

ORDER BY 3 DESC;

docs.title: Object Counts - Tables
docs.text:
SELECT table_name

FROM information_schema.tables

WHERE table_schema IN ('main', 'ginarchive', 'ginview', 'gateway')

AND table_type IN ('FOREIGN', 'BASE TABLE')

ORDER BY table_name;

docs.title: Object Counts - Primary Keys
docs.text:
SELECT c.table_schema, c.table_name, c.constraint_name

FROM information_schema.table_constraints c

WHERE c.constraint_type = 'PRIMARY KEY'

AND c.table_schema IN ('main', 'ginview', 'ginarchive', 'gateway')

ORDER BY c.table_name;

docs.title: Object Counts - Views
docs.text:
SELECT table_name

FROM information_schema.views

WHERE table_schema IN ('main', 'ginarchive', 'gateway', 'ginview')

ORDER BY table_name;

docs.title: Object Counts - Triggers
docs.text:
SELECT trigger_name, event_manipulation AS event, event_object_table AS table_name,

action_statement AS trigger_body, action_timing AS trigger_timing

FROM information_schema.triggers

WHERE trigger_schema IN ('main', 'ginarchive', 'ginview', 'gateway')

ORDER BY trigger_name;

docs.title: Object Counts - Sequences
docs.text:
SELECT sequence_name

FROM information_schema.sequences

WHERE sequence_schema IN ('main', 'ginview', 'gateway', 'ginarchive')

ORDER BY sequence_name;

docs.title: Object Counts - Functions
docs.text:
SELECT routine_name

FROM information_schema.routines

WHERE routine_type = 'FUNCTION'

AND routine_schema IN ('main', 'ginview', 'gateway', 'ginarchive');

docs.title: Useful Sizing Functions - Quick Reference
docs.text:
-- pg_size_pretty() formats byte sizes as human readable

-- pg_relation_size() size of a table/index (no TOAST/index)

-- pg_total_relation_size() total size incl. indexes and TOAST

-- pg_database_size() size of a database

-- pg_indexes_size() total size of all indexes on a table

-- pg_tablespace_size() size of a tablespace

-- pg_column_size() size of a value of a specific column/type

docs.title: Top 5 Queries by Mean Execution Time
docs.text:
SELECT userid::regrole, dbid, mean_exec_time, query

FROM pg_stat_statements

ORDER BY mean_exec_time DESC

LIMIT 5;

docs.title: Top 5 Queries by Total Execution Time
docs.text:
SELECT userid::regrole, dbid, query

FROM pg_stat_statements

ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC

LIMIT 5;

docs.title: Top 10 Queries by Total Time with % CPU Share
docs.text:
SELECT substring(query, 1, 200) AS query,

round((100 * total_exec_time / sum(total_exec_time) OVER ())::numeric, 2) AS percent,

round(total_exec_time::numeric, 2) AS total,

calls,

round(mean_exec_time::numeric, 2) AS mean

FROM pg_stat_statements

ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC

LIMIT 10;

docs.title: Queries with Highest I/O Wait Time
docs.text:
SELECT userid::regrole, dbid, query, queryid, mean_exec_time / 1000 AS mean_time_seconds

FROM pg_stat_statements

ORDER BY (blk_read_time + blk_write_time) DESC

LIMIT 10;

docs.title: Top Time-Consuming Queries (full breakdown)
docs.text:
SELECT userid::regrole, dbid, query, calls,

total_exec_time / 1000 AS total_time_seconds,

min_exec_time / 1000 AS min_time_seconds,

max_exec_time / 1000 AS max_time_seconds,

mean_exec_time / 1000 AS mean_time_seconds

FROM pg_stat_statements

ORDER BY mean_exec_time DESC

LIMIT 10;

docs.title: Queries with High Memory / Shared Buffer Usage
docs.text:
SELECT userid::regrole, dbid, queryid, query

FROM pg_stat_statements

ORDER BY (shared_blks_hit + shared_blks_dirtied) DESC

LIMIT 10;

docs.title: Queries Doing the Most Buffer Writes
docs.text:
SELECT query, shared_blks_dirtied

FROM pg_stat_statements

WHERE shared_blks_dirtied > 0

ORDER BY 2 DESC;

docs.title: Queries with the Highest Block Read Time
docs.text:
SELECT * FROM pg_stat_statements

WHERE blk_read_time <> 0

ORDER BY blk_read_time DESC;

docs.title: Average Statement Execution Time (cluster-wide)
docs.text:
SELECT (sum(total_exec_time) / sum(calls))::numeric(6,3)

FROM pg_stat_statements;

docs.title: Reset pg_stat_statements
docs.text:
SELECT pg_stat_statements_reset();

SELECT count(*) FROM pg_stat_statements;

docs.title: Replication Status
docs.text: SELECT * FROM pg_stat_replication;

docs.title: Replication Lag in Seconds
docs.text:
SELECT ROUND(EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM replay_lag)) AS lag_seconds

FROM pg_stat_replication

WHERE application_name = 'walreceiver';

docs.title: Replication Slot Information
docs.text: SELECT * FROM pg_replication_slots;

docs.title: Logical Replication Slot Lag Detail
docs.text:
SELECT

s.slot_name, s.active,

ROUND(pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), s.restart_lsn) / 1048576.0, 2) || ' MB' AS slot_lag_size,

pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), s.restart_lsn) AS slot_lag_bytes,

ROUND(pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), s.confirmed_flush_lsn) / 1048576.0, 2) || ' MB' AS consumer_lag_size,

pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), s.confirmed_flush_lsn) AS consumer_lag_bytes,

s.slot_type, s.database, r.replay_lag, r.write_lag, r.flush_lag

FROM pg_replication_slots s

LEFT JOIN pg_stat_replication r ON s.active_pid = r.pid

WHERE s.slot_type = 'logical'

ORDER BY slot_lag_bytes DESC NULLS LAST;

docs.title: WAL Directory Size (MB)
docs.text: SELECT (sum(size))::BIGINT / 1024 / 1024 AS wal_size_mb FROM pg_ls_waldir();

docs.title: WAL Archiver Status
docs.text: SELECT * FROM pg_stat_archiver;

docs.title: WAL Archiving Gap (current vs last archived)
docs.text:
SELECT pg_walfile_name(pg_current_wal_lsn()), last_archived_wal, last_failed_wal,

('x' || substring(pg_walfile_name(pg_current_wal_lsn()), 9, 8))::bit(32)::int * 256

\+ ('x' || substring(pg_walfile_name(pg_current_wal_lsn()), 17))::bit(32)::int

\- ('x' || substring(last_archived_wal, 9, 8))::bit(32)::int * 256

\- ('x' || substring(last_archived_wal, 17))::bit(32)::int AS diff

FROM pg_stat_archiver;

docs.title: Cron Job Counts per Database
docs.text: SELECT database, count(jobid) FROM cron.job GROUP BY database;

docs.title: Today's Cron Job Run Status per Database
docs.text:
SELECT database, status, count(status)

FROM cron.job_run_details

WHERE end_time::DATE = CURRENT_DATE::DATE

GROUP BY database, status;

docs.title: List Prepared/Orphaned Transactions
docs.text:
SELECT gid, prepared, owner, database, transaction

FROM pg_prepared_xacts

ORDER BY age(transaction) DESC;

docs.title: Find Locks Held by Prepared Transactions
docs.text:
SELECT px.gid, px.owner, px.prepared, l.locktype, l.mode, l.granted, c.relname AS object_name

FROM pg_prepared_xacts px

JOIN pg_locks l ON px.transaction = l.transactionid

LEFT JOIN pg_class c ON l.relation = c.oid;

docs.title: Resolve a Prepared Transaction
docs.text:
COMMIT PREPARED '<gid>';

-- or

ROLLBACK PREPARED '<gid>';

docs.title: Reindex a Database
docs.text: REINDEX (VERBOSE) DATABASE <database_name>;

docs.title: Reload Configuration (without restart)
docs.text: SELECT pg_reload_conf();

SELECT * FROM query_store.qs_view;

SELECT * FROM query_store.pgms_wait_sampling_view;

SELECT * FROM query_store.query_texts_view;

SELECT * FROM query_store.query_plans_view;

docs.text: Command Description \c dbname Switch connection to a database \l / \l+ List databases (with extra info) \dt List tables \d table_name Describe a table \dn List schemas \df List functions \dv List views \du List users/roles \ds List sequences \g Execute previous command \s Command history \s filename Save command history to file \? Help on psql commands \timing Toggle query execution timing \e Edit statement in external editor \ef Edit function in external editor \a Toggle aligned/non-aligned output \H Toggle HTML output format \conninfo Show current connection info \db List tablespaces \x Toggle expanded display \q Quit psql \! cls Clear terminal (Windows) \! clear Clear terminal (Linux) \! df -h Run an OS-level command (e.g. disk usage)

docs.title: Historical Database Size (for a given day)
docs.text:
SELECT INSTANCE_NAME, LOGDATE, DATABASE, SIZE_GB AS SIZE

FROM DATABASESIZE_INFORMATION

WHERE LOGDATE::date = CURRENT_DATE::date

AND DATABASE LIKE '%-PROD'

AND DATABASE NOT LIKE 'ZZZ%'

AND instance_name = '<instance_name>'

ORDER BY SIZE_GB DESC;

docs.title: Database Growth Comparison (two dates)
docs.text:
SELECT

t."Instance_Name", t.database,

MAX(t."NEWDATE") AS "NEWDATE", round(SUM(t.newsize) / 1024, 2) AS newsize,

MAX(t."OLDDATE") AS "OLDDATE", round(SUM(t.oldsize) / 1024, 2) AS oldsize,

round(SUM(t.newsize - t.oldsize) / 1024, 2) AS diff

FROM (

SELECT n.instance_name AS "Instance_Name", n.database,

n.logdate::date AS "NEWDATE", NULL::date AS "OLDDATE",

COALESCE(n.size_mb, 0) AS newsize, 0 AS oldsize

FROM public.databasesize_information AS n

WHERE n.logdate::date = '<new_date>' AND n.instance_name = '<instance_name>'

UNION ALL

SELECT o.instance_name, o.database,

NULL::date AS "NEWDATE", o.logdate::date AS "OLDDATE",

0 AS newsize, COALESCE(o.size_mb, 0) AS oldsize

FROM public.databasesize_information AS o

WHERE o.logdate::date = '<old_date>' AND o.instance_name = '<instance_name>'

) t

WHERE t.database LIKE '<database_name>'

GROUP BY t.database, t."Instance_Name"

HAVING SUM(t.newsize - t.oldsize) <> 0

ORDER BY diff DESC;

docs.title: Top Size-Consuming Segments (historical, > 1000 MB)
docs.text:
SELECT instance_name, logdate, database_name, schema_name, object_name, object_type, object_size, size_mb

FROM public.object_segment_selfhosted4

WHERE logdate::date = '<log_date>'

AND size_mb > 1000

ORDER BY size_mb DESC;

docs.title: Object Growth Comparison (two dates)
docs.text:
SELECT

t."Instance_Name", t."database_name", t."object_name",

MAX(t."NEWDATE") AS "NEWDATE", SUM(t.newsize) AS newsize,

MAX(t."OLDDATE") AS "OLDDATE", SUM(t.oldsize) AS oldsize,

SUM(t.newsize - t.oldsize) AS diff

FROM (

SELECT n.instance_name AS "Instance_Name", n.database_name, n.object_name,

n.logdate::date AS "NEWDATE", NULL::date AS "OLDDATE",

COALESCE(n.size_mb, 0) AS newsize, 0 AS oldsize

FROM public.object_segment_edb1 AS n

WHERE n.logdate::date = '<new_date>' AND n.instance_name = '<instance_name>'

UNION ALL

SELECT o.instance_name, o.database_name, o.object_name,

NULL::date AS "NEWDATE", o.logdate::date AS "OLDDATE",

0 AS newsize, COALESCE(o.size_mb, 0) AS oldsize

FROM public.object_segment_edb1 AS o

WHERE o.logdate::date = '<old_date>' AND o.instance_name = '<instance_name>'

) t

WHERE t.database_name LIKE '<database_name>'

GROUP BY t.object_name, t."Instance_Name", t."database_name"

HAVING SUM(t.newsize - t.oldsize) <> 0

ORDER BY diff DESC;

docs.title: Temp Spilling on Disk [total spill by database]
docs.text:
SELECT
          COALESCE(a.datname, 'unattributed') AS database_name,
          sum(t.size)::BIGINT AS temp_bytes,
          count(*) AS temp_file_count
      FROM pg_ls_tmpdir() t
      LEFT JOIN pg_stat_activity a
          ON a.pid = substring(t.name FROM 'pgsql_tmp(\d+)')::int
      GROUP BY a.datname
      ORDER BY temp_bytes DESC;

docs.title: Temp Spilling on Disk [query spilling temp on disk]
docs.text:
SELECT
    a.datname AS database_name,
    a.pid,
    a.usename,
    a.query,
    a.state,
    round(sum(t.size) / (1024.0 * 1024 * 1024), 2) AS temp_size_gb,
    count(*) AS temp_file_count
FROM pg_ls_tmpdir() t
LEFT JOIN pg_stat_activity a
    ON a.pid = substring(t.name FROM 'pgsql_tmp(\d+)')::int
GROUP BY a.datname, a.pid, a.usename, a.query, a.state
ORDER BY temp_size_gb DESC;

docs.title: What is PostgreSQL?
docs.text:
• PostgreSQL is a free, open-source object-relational database management system (ORDBMS).
  • It began in 1986 as the POSTGRES research project at the University of California, Berkeley, led by Professor Michael Stonebraker.
  • It is cross-platform and runs on Linux, FreeBSD, macOS, Solaris and Microsoft Windows.
  • It provides fully ACID transactions (Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability).
  • It manages concurrency through MVCC (Multiversion Concurrency Control): readers never block writers and writers never block readers.

About this guide: the commands target PostgreSQL 17 (latest minor release 17.11, August 2026). Many screenshots were captured on lab systems running PostgreSQL 12, 13 or 14, so version numbers and paths in the images may show 12, 13 or 14. The steps are the same in PostgreSQL 17 unless the text says otherwise; always use the commands in the text. Chapter 16 describes what is new in PostgreSQL 17.

docs.title: PostgreSQL Terminology
docs.text:
PostgreSQL documentation uses its own names for several common database terms:

Common name PostgreSQL name Table or index Relation Row Tuple Column Attribute Data block (on disk) Page Page (in memory) Buffer

docs.title: PostgreSQL Limits
docs.text: Item Upper limit Comment Database size Unlimited Number of databases 4,294,950,911 Relations per database 1,431,650,303 Relation size 32 TB With the default block size (BLCKSZ) of 8192 bytes Rows per table Limited by the number of tuples that fit on 4,294,967,295 pages Columns per table 1,600 Further limited by the tuple size fitting in one page Field size 1 GB Identifier length 63 bytes Can be raised by recompiling Indexes per table Unlimited Constrained by relations per database Columns per index 32 Partition keys 32

docs.title: Page Layout
docs.text:
• A page is the smallest unit of data storage.
  • Every table and index is stored as an array of fixed-size pages.
  • The default page size is 8 kB. A different size can only be chosen when compiling the server.
  • All pages of a table are logically equivalent; any row can be stored in any page.
Item Description PageHeaderData 24 bytes long. General information about the page, including free-space pointers. ItemIdData Array of item identifiers (line pointers) pointing to the actual items. 4 bytes per item. Free space Unallocated space. New item pointers are allocated from the start of this area, new items from the end. Items (tuples) The actual rows themselves. Special space Access-method-specific data (used by indexes). Empty in ordinary tables.

docs.title: 2. Installing PostgreSQL on Windows and Linux
System Requirements
docs.text:
Hardware (minimum for a lab system)

  • 1 GHz processor
  • 2 GB RAM
  • 512 MB of free disk space for the software, plus space for your data

Software

  • Administrator privileges on Windows
  • root or sudo access on Linux

docs.title: Installing PostgreSQL 17 on Windows
docs.text:
1. Go to https://www.postgresql.org/download/ and choose Windows.
  2. Click Download the installer.
  3. Choose the latest PostgreSQL 17 release for Windows x86-64 (for example 17.11). Always install the newest minor release: it contains all security and bug fixes (see Chapter 16).
  4. Right-click the downloaded setup file and choose Run as administrator.
  5. Follow the wizard: choose the installation directory, data directory, superuser password, port (default 5432) and components.
  6. Wait for the installation to complete.
  7. Open SQL Shell (psql) from the Start menu, or connect from a command prompt:
psql -U <username> -d <database_name> -p <port_number>

docs.title: Setting Up the Windows Environment
docs.text:
1. Click Start, search for This PC, right-click it and choose Properties.
  1. Click Advanced system settings.
  2. In System Properties, click Environment Variables.
  1. Under System variables, select Path and click Edit.
  1. Click New and add the PostgreSQL bin folder, for example D:\PostgreSQL\17\bin. Click OK.
  2. Back in Environment Variables, click New under System variables.
  3. Enter PGDATA as the variable name and the data directory as the value, for example D:\PostgreSQL\17\data.
  4. Click OK to save and close all windows. Open a new command prompt for the changes to apply.

docs.title: Installing PostgreSQL on Linux (Default Directory)
docs.text:
These steps use the PostgreSQL (PGDG) YUM repository on Red Hat Enterprise Linux 8. For RHEL 9 (or Rocky/AlmaLinux 9), replace EL-8 with EL-9 in the repository URL; the module-disable step is not needed on RHEL 9.

  1. Go to https://www.postgresql.org/download/ and choose Linux → Red Hat/Rocky/AlmaLinux.
  2. In the PostgreSQL Yum Repository section, choose version 17, platform RHEL 8 and architecture x86_64. A setup script is generated.

  1. Install the repository RPM:
sudo dnf install -y https://download.postgresql.org/pub/repos/yum/reporpms/EL-8-x86_64/pgdg-redhat-repo-latest.noarch.rpm

  1. Disable the built-in PostgreSQL module (RHEL 8 only) and install the server:
sudo dnf -qy module disable postgresql
sudo dnf install -y postgresql17-server

  1. Initialise the cluster, enable automatic start and start the service. PGSETUP_INITDB_OPTIONS passes extra options to initdb; here it enables data checksums:
sudo PGSETUP_INITDB_OPTIONS="--data-checksums" /usr/pgsql-17/bin/postgresql-17-setup initdb
sudo systemctl enable postgresql-17
sudo systemctl start postgresql-17
sudo systemctl status postgresql-17

Note: these steps install the binaries in /usr/pgsql-17 and create the data directory at /var/lib/pgsql/17/data.

docs.title: Setting Up the Linux Environment (Default Directory)
docs.text:
1. The OS user postgres is created automatically during installation. Set its password:
sudo passwd postgres
  1. Switch to the postgres user:
su - postgres
  1. Edit the postgres user’s profile:
vi ~/.bash_profile
  1. Add the following lines:
[ -f /etc/profile ] && source /etc/profile
PGDATA=/var/lib/pgsql/17/data
export PGDATA

# If you want to customize your settings, use the file below.
# It is not overridden by the RPMs.
[ -f /var/lib/pgsql/.pgsql_profile ] && source /var/lib/pgsql/.pgsql_profile

export PATH=/usr/pgsql-17/bin:$HOME/bin:$PATH
  1. Save the file and load it into the current session:
. ~/.bash_profile

docs.title: Installing PostgreSQL on Linux (Non-Default Directory)
docs.text:
1. Add the PGDG repository and install the server exactly as in steps 1–4 of the default installation.
  1. Create the new data directory, for example /u01/pgsql/17/data, with the correct owner and permissions:
sudo mkdir -p /u01/pgsql/17/data
sudo chown -R postgres:postgres /u01/pgsql
sudo chmod 700 /u01/pgsql/17/data
  1. Point the service at the new directory. Use a systemd drop-in file rather than editing /lib/systemd/system/postgresql-17.service directly, because package updates overwrite that file:
sudo systemctl edit postgresql-17

Add these lines and save:

[Service]
# Location of database directory
Environment=PGDATA=/u01/pgsql/17/data/

  1. Reload systemd:
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
  1. Initialise the cluster, enable automatic start and start the service:
sudo /usr/pgsql-17/bin/postgresql-17-setup initdb
sudo systemctl enable postgresql-17
sudo systemctl start postgresql-17
sudo systemctl status postgresql-17

docs.title: Setting Up the Linux Environment (Non-Default Directory)
docs.text:
Follow the same steps as for the default directory (set the password, su - postgres, edit ~/.bash_profile).

The only difference is the PGDATA value:

[ -f /etc/profile ] && source /etc/profile
PGDATA=/u01/pgsql/17/data
export PGDATA

[ -f /var/lib/pgsql/.pgsql_profile ] && source /var/lib/pgsql/.pgsql_profile

export PATH=/usr/pgsql-17/bin:$HOME/bin:$PATH

Load the profile with . ~/.bash_profile.

docs.title: Fundamentals of PostgreSQL Architecture
docs.text:
• PostgreSQL is a relational database management system with a client-server architecture.
  • It uses a process-per-connection model: each client connection is served by its own server process.
  • A set of processes and shared memory structures together form an instance.
  • Client programs connect to the instance and request read and write operations.
  • The default port is 5432.

docs.title: Postmaster (supervisor process)
docs.text:
• The postmaster is the first process started when PostgreSQL starts.
  • It supervises the other processes and restarts them if they fail.
  • It listens on the configured address and port for new connection requests.
  • For every new connection it forks a new backend process (named postgres). The backend authenticates the client using pg_hba.conf and then serves all of that client’s queries.

docs.title: Background (utility) processes
docs.text:
Process Role Background writer Periodically writes dirty buffers from shared buffers to the data files, so backends rarely have to. WAL writer Flushes the WAL buffers to the WAL files on disk. Checkpointer Runs a checkpoint every checkpoint_timeout (default 5 minutes) or when max_wal_size is about to be exceeded, writing all dirty buffers to the data files. Autovacuum launcher Starts autovacuum worker processes that vacuum and analyse tables (if autovacuum = on, the default). Startup process Replays WAL during crash recovery, and continuously on a standby. Logical replication launcher Starts the apply workers for logical replication subscriptions. WAL summarizer (PG 17) When summarize_wal = on, records which blocks each WAL range changed (in pg_wal/summaries). Needed for incremental backups. Slot sync worker (PG 17) On a standby with sync_replication_slots = on, copies failover-enabled logical slots from the primary. Logger (logging collector) Writes server messages to the log files (if logging_collector = on). Archiver (optional) When archive_mode = on, copies completed WAL segments to the archive location. WAL sender / WAL receiver Used by replication: the sender runs on the primary, the receiver on the standby.

No statistics collector process since PostgreSQL 15. Activity statistics (table and index access counts, dead rows and so on, shown in the pg_stat_* views and used by autovacuum) are kept in shared memory by each backend and written to pg_stat at shutdown. Planner statistics (data distribution used to choose query plans) are a separate thing: they are gathered by ANALYZE and stored in pg_statistic.

docs.title: Memory Segments
docs.text: Area Scope Parameter Used for Shared buffers Shared shared_buffers Cache of table and index pages WAL buffers Shared wal_buffers WAL records not yet written to disk CLOG buffers Shared (automatic) Commit status of transactions (pg_xact) Work memory Per operation work_mem Sorts and hash tables (ORDER BY, DISTINCT, hash joins, hash aggregates) Maintenance work memory Per operation maintenance_work_mem VACUUM, CREATE INDEX, ALTER TABLE ADD FOREIGN KEY SLRU buffers (PG 17) Shared transaction_buffers, subtransaction_buffers, multixact_*_buffers, … Caches for commit status, subtransactions, multixacts and more; sizes are configurable from PG 17 Temp buffers Per session temp_buffers Pages of temporary tables only

docs.title: Shared buffers
docs.text:
• Backends never read or write data files directly; all reads and changes go through the shared buffer area.
  • A page changed in memory but not yet written to disk is called a dirty page.
  • Dirty pages are written to the data files by the background writer and the checkpointer.
  • Size is set by shared_buffers in postgresql.conf (restart required).

docs.title: WAL buffers
docs.text:
• Also called transaction log buffers.
  • WAL (write-ahead log) records describe every change to the data and are sufficient to reconstruct the data during recovery.
  • WAL is written to a series of 16 MB files called WAL segments in pg_wal.
  • WAL buffers are flushed to the WAL segments by the WAL writer and at every transaction commit.
  • Size is set by wal_buffers.

docs.title: CLOG and other buffers
docs.text:
• CLOG (“commit log”, stored in pg_xact) records the status of every transaction: in progress, committed or aborted. CLOG buffers cache these pages in memory.
  • Work memory (work_mem) is used by a single sort or hash operation (hash operations may use work_mem × hash_mem_multiplier, default 2.0). A complex query can use several multiples of it at once.
  • Maintenance work memory (maintenance_work_mem) is used by maintenance commands.
  • Temp buffers (temp_buffers) cache the pages of temporary tables created by a session. Large sorts and hashes that exceed work_mem spill to temporary files, not to temp buffers.

docs.title: Physical Files
docs.text:
• Data files: store table and index data.
  • WAL files: every change is written here first, before the change is considered committed.
  • Log files: server messages (stderr, csvlog or syslog output).
  • Archived WAL files (optional): copies of WAL segments kept for point-in-time recovery and standby servers.

Parameters related to memory and WAL: shared_buffers, wal_buffers, work_mem, maintenance_work_mem, temp_buffers, max_wal_size.

docs.title: What Is a Database Cluster?
docs.text:
• A database cluster is a collection of databases managed by a single PostgreSQL instance (one postmaster, one port, one data directory).
  • initdb creates a new cluster.
  • Creating a cluster means creating the data directory and the files inside it.
  • The storage area must be initialised before the server can be started.
  • Default data directory locations (not mandatory):
  • Linux (PGDG packages): /var/lib/pgsql/17/data
  • Windows: C:\Program Files\PostgreSQL\17\data

docs.title: initdb
docs.text:
• initdb is the command-line utility that initialises a new cluster: it creates the directory structure, the system catalogs and the template0, template1 and postgres databases.
  • Run it as the OS user that will own the server process (normally postgres), never as root.
  • It can be run directly, or through pg_ctl initdb.
# Linux
initdb -D /var/lib/pgsql/17/data -U postgres -W -E UTF8 --data-checksums
pg_ctl initdb -D /var/lib/pgsql/17/data -o "-U postgres -W -E UTF8 --data-checksums"
:: Windows
initdb -D "D:\PostgreSQL\17\data" -U postgres -W -E UTF8 --data-checksums
pg_ctl initdb -D "D:\PostgreSQL\17\data" -o "-U postgres -W -E UTF8 --data-checksums"
Option Meaning -D Data directory location -U Name of the database superuser for the new cluster -W Prompt for the superuser’s password -E Default encoding (use UTF8) -k, --data-checksums Enable data page checksums to detect storage corruption. Recommended; off by default in PG 17 (on by default from PG 18). Also lets pg_rewind work without wal_log_hints. --locale-provider libc (default), icu, or builtin (new in PG 17, e.g. --locale-provider=builtin --builtin-locale=C.UTF-8 for fast, OS-independent sorting).

docs.title: Starting and Stopping a Cluster
docs.text:
# Linux (systemd service)
sudo systemctl start postgresql-17
sudo systemctl stop postgresql-17

# Linux (as the postgres user)
pg_ctl start -D /var/lib/pgsql/17/data
pg_ctl stop  -D /var/lib/pgsql/17/data -m fast
:: Windows
pg_ctl start -D "C:\Program Files\PostgreSQL\17\data"
pg_ctl stop  -D "C:\Program Files\PostgreSQL\17\data" -m smart
pg_ctl stop  -D "C:\Program Files\PostgreSQL\17\data" -m fast
pg_ctl stop  -D "C:\Program Files\PostgreSQL\17\data" -m immediate

If PGDATA is set, -D can be omitted.

docs.title: Types of Shutdown
docs.text: Mode Behaviour smart Refuses new connections and waits for all existing sessions to end, then shuts down. fast (default) Refuses new connections, rolls back open transactions, disconnects clients and shuts down cleanly. immediate Aborts all processes without a clean shutdown. Crash recovery runs at the next start.

docs.title: Reload vs Restart
docs.text:
• After changing server parameters, the configuration must be reloaded or the server restarted for the change to take effect.
  • A reload re-reads the configuration files without stopping the server. Most parameters take effect this way.
  • Some parameters (for example shared_buffers, max_connections, listen_addresses, wal_level) only take effect after a restart. They are marked # (change requires restart) in postgresql.conf, and have context = 'postmaster' in pg_settings.
  • A restart shuts down all activity, releases resources, closes all files and starts again with the new configuration.
# Reload
sudo systemctl reload postgresql-17          # Linux
pg_ctl reload -D "D:\PostgreSQL\17\data"     # Windows (or Linux as postgres)

# Restart
sudo systemctl restart postgresql-17         # Linux
pg_ctl restart -D "D:\PostgreSQL\17\data"    # Windows (or Linux as postgres)

From psql (any platform), a reload can also be triggered with:

SELECT pg_reload_conf();

docs.title: pg_controldata
docs.text:
pg_controldata displays control information about a cluster: version, cluster state, latest checkpoint location, WAL settings and more. It works even when the server is stopped.

/usr/pgsql-17/bin/pg_controldata -D /var/lib/pgsql/17/data     # Linux
pg_controldata -D "D:\PostgreSQL\17\data"                       # Windows

docs.title: Installation Directory Layout
docs.text:
• Linux (PGDG packages): binaries in /usr/pgsql-17, data in /var/lib/pgsql/17/data. Source builds default to /usr/local/pgsql.
  • Windows: C:\Program Files\PostgreSQL\<version> by default.
Folder Contents bin Programs (psql, initdb, pg_ctl, createdb, createuser, pg_dump and others) data Data directory (Windows default) doc Documentation include C header files installer Installer files scripts Helper scripts such as runpsql and server-control scripts share Sample configuration files, time zone data, extension files pgAdmin 4 pgAdmin files

docs.title: Data Directory Layout
docs.text: Item Description base One subdirectory per database, named after the database OID global Cluster-wide tables such as pg_database, pg_authid and pg_tablespace pg_commit_ts Transaction commit timestamps (when track_commit_timestamp = on) pg_dynshmem Files used by the dynamic shared memory subsystem pg_logical Status data for logical decoding pg_multixact Multitransaction status data (used for shared row locks) pg_notify LISTEN/NOTIFY status data pg_replslot Replication slot data pg_serial Information about committed serializable transactions pg_snapshots Exported snapshots pg_stat Activity statistics saved at clean shutdown and reloaded at startup pg_stat_tmp Temporary files for extensions such as pg_stat_statements (no longer used by the server itself since PG 15) pg_subtrans Subtransaction status data pg_tblspc Symbolic links to tablespaces pg_twophase State files for prepared transactions pg_wal WAL (write-ahead log) files. pg_wal/summaries holds WAL summaries for incremental backup (PG 17). pg_xact Transaction commit status data (CLOG) log Server log files (default log_directory) current_logfiles Records the log file(s) currently being written by the logging collector postgresql.conf Main configuration file postgresql.auto.conf Parameters set with ALTER SYSTEM pg_hba.conf Client authentication rules pg_ident.conf User name maps (OS user → database user) postmaster.opts Command-line options the server was last started with postmaster.pid Lock file with the postmaster PID, data directory, start time, port, socket directory, listen address and shared memory ID. Not present after shutdown. PG_VERSION Major version number of PostgreSQL

docs.title: The base Directory
docs.text:
• Each database is a subdirectory named after its object identifier (OID).
  • template1 always has OID 1. Since PostgreSQL 15, template0 always has OID 4 and postgres has OID 5.
  • To find database OIDs:
SELECT oid, datname FROM pg_database;

docs.title: postgresql.conf
docs.text:
• postgresql.conf holds the parameters that configure the server and control its performance.
  • initdb creates a default copy in the data directory.
  • The file has one name = value parameter per line; lines starting with # are comments.
  • Parameters that need a restart are marked # (change requires restart).

docs.title: Catalog Views for Viewing Settings
docs.text:
• pg_settings shows the current run-time value of every parameter. It is an alternative to the SHOW command, with extra columns such as unit, context (when a change takes effect) and source.
  • pg_file_settings summarises the contents of the configuration files. It is useful to check whether planned changes in the files are valid before reloading. Each name = value entry has an applied column and, if it cannot be applied, an error column.
  • In short: pg_settings shows what the server is using now; pg_file_settings shows what is written in the files.
SELECT name, setting, unit, context FROM pg_settings;

To check a single parameter, for example archive_mode, use either method:

SELECT name, setting FROM pg_settings WHERE name = 'archive_mode';
SHOW archive_mode;

docs.title: Changing a Parameter in postgresql.conf
docs.text:
1. Check the current value.
  2. Back up the file before editing it.
  3. Remove the leading # from the parameter if it is commented out.
  4. Check whether the parameter needs a restart.
  5. Set the new value.
  6. Reload or restart PostgreSQL as required.
  7. Verify the value with SHOW or pg_settings.

Example: change shared_buffers from 200 MB to 250 MB and work_mem from 10 MB to 20 MB.

Step 1. Check the current values.

Step 2. Open <data directory>\postgresql.conf and edit both parameters.

Note: the file shows that shared_buffers requires a restart, while work_mem does not.

Step 3. Save the file and reload the configuration from psql:

SELECT pg_reload_conf();

The function returns true if the reload signal was sent. Parameters that do not need a restart (here work_mem) take effect immediately for new and existing sessions.

Step 4. shared_buffers still shows the old value because it requires a restart. Restart the server:

pg_ctl restart -D "D:\PostgreSQL\17\data"

docs.title: postgresql.auto.conf
docs.text:
• This file holds settings made with the ALTER SYSTEM command. Do not edit it by hand.
  • Values in postgresql.auto.conf override the same parameters in postgresql.conf.
  • ALTER SYSTEM provides a SQL interface for changing server-wide defaults.
ALTER SYSTEM SET configuration_parameter = 'value';
ALTER SYSTEM RESET configuration_parameter;
ALTER SYSTEM RESET ALL;

Example: change shared_buffers and work_mem with ALTER SYSTEM.

Step 1. Set the parameters:

ALTER SYSTEM SET shared_buffers = '250MB';
ALTER SYSTEM SET work_mem = '20MB';

Step 2. Reload the configuration:

SELECT pg_reload_conf();

Step 3. Open postgresql.conf. It is unchanged, because ALTER SYSTEM writes only to postgresql.auto.conf.

Step 4. Query pg_file_settings to see whether the planned changes will work:

SELECT sourcefile, name, setting, applied, error FROM pg_file_settings;

The last two rows show shared_buffers and work_mem from postgresql.auto.conf. The applied column shows whether the value is in effect. shared_buffers shows setting could not be applied because it still needs a restart.

Step 5. To roll back one or all ALTER SYSTEM changes:

ALTER SYSTEM RESET shared_buffers;
ALTER SYSTEM RESET ALL;

Then reload (or restart, for restart-only parameters).

Note: when the same parameter appears in both files, PostgreSQL uses the value from postgresql.auto.conf, because that file is read last.

PostgreSQL 17 – allow_alter_system: if configuration is managed by an external tool (Ansible, Patroni, a cloud control plane), set allow_alter_system = off in postgresql.conf so that ALTER SYSTEM is refused. This is a guard against accidental changes, not a security boundary: superusers can still change files in other ways.

docs.title: pg_ident.conf
docs.text:
pg_ident.conf maps external (operating system or certificate) user names to PostgreSQL user names.

  • The OS user that starts a connection is not necessarily the same as the database user.
  • A map is used together with an authentication method in pg_hba.conf (for example peer, ident, cert or gss) by adding map=<mapname> to the pg_hba.conf line.
  • The file is read at startup and on every reload (pg_ctl reload or SELECT pg_reload_conf();).
  • From PostgreSQL 16, check the loaded mappings and any errors with SELECT * FROM pg_ident_file_mappings;.

Sample

# MAPNAME   SYSTEM-USERNAME   PG-USERNAME
sales       admin             sales
sales       sagar             sales
test        sagar             postgres
  • MAPNAME is any name; it is referenced from pg_hba.conf.
  • SYSTEM-USERNAME is the user name detected for the client.
  • PG-USERNAME is the PostgreSQL user the client may connect as.
  • With map sales, OS users admin and sagar may connect as database user sales. With map test, OS user sagar may connect as postgres.

docs.title: pg_hba.conf
docs.text:
• Controls client authentication (HBA = host-based authentication).
  • When a connection request arrives, PostgreSQL reads the lines from top to bottom and uses the first line that matches the connection type, database, user and client address.
  • If no line matches, the connection is rejected.
  • The file controls which hosts may connect, how clients authenticate, which database users they may use and which databases they may access.
  • Changes need only a reload, not a restart.
  • From PostgreSQL 16, database and user columns accept regular expressions (prefixed with /), and the file can pull in other files with include, include_if_exists and include_dir.

Sample

# TYPE    DATABASE      USER      ADDRESS            METHOD
local     all           all                          peer
host      all           all       127.0.0.1/32       scram-sha-256
host      all           all       ::1/128            scram-sha-256
hostssl   sales         sales     192.168.4.0/24     scram-sha-256
host      all           all       10.10.0.15/32      reject
host      replication   repuser   192.168.4.153/32   scram-sha-256

docs.title: Column 1 – Connection type
docs.text: Type Meaning local Connections through a Unix-domain socket on the same machine. No address column. (Not used on Windows.) host TCP/IP connections, with or without SSL. The server must listen on the address (listen_addresses). hostssl TCP/IP connections that use SSL only. hostnossl TCP/IP connections that do not use SSL. hostgssenc TCP/IP connections that use GSSAPI encryption. hostnogssenc TCP/IP connections that do not use GSSAPI encryption.

docs.title: Column 2 – Database
docs.text:
• all – matches all databases.
  • sameuser – the database name must equal the user name.
  • samerole – the user must be a member of a role with the same name as the database.
  • replication – matches physical replication connections (logical replication connections match the database name instead).
  • A database name, or a comma-separated list of names.

docs.title: Column 3 – User
docs.text:
• The database user name (not the OS user).
  • all, a user name, a group (role) name prefixed with +, or a comma-separated list.

Note: database and user names that contain spaces, commas, quotes or other special characters must be quoted. Quoting a keyword such as "all", "sameuser" or "replication" makes it match a database or user with that literal name.

docs.title: Column 4 – Address
docs.text:
• A host name, or an IP address with a CIDR mask, for example 192.168.4.10/32 (one host) or 192.168.4.0/24 (a whole subnet).
  • Alternatively, an IP address and a netmask in two columns; for a single host the netmask is 255.255.255.255.
  • local lines have no address column.

docs.title: Column 5 – Authentication method
docs.text:
Method Description trust Allows the connection without a password. Use only on fully trusted machines. reject Always rejects the connection. Useful to block specific hosts or users ahead of broader rules. scram-sha-256 Challenge-response password authentication. Recommended, and the default password_encryption since PostgreSQL 14. md5 Older hashed-password method. Still works in PG 17, but is weaker than SCRAM (a timing side-channel was fixed in 17.10, CVE-2026-6478) and is deprecated from PG 18. Migrate users to SCRAM (see note below). password Sends the password in clear text. Avoid unless the connection is SSL-encrypted. peer local only: uses the OS user name of the client process. ident Uses an ident server on the client host to get the OS user name (TCP/IP only). gss, sspi Kerberos (GSSAPI) and Windows single sign-on. ldap, radius, pam, cert, bsd External authentication services and client certificates.

ident, peer, cert and gss can use a user name map from pg_ident.conf via the map= option.

Moving users from MD5 to SCRAM: make sure password_encryption = 'scram-sha-256' (the default), have each user set their password again (\password username in psql), then change md5 to scram-sha-256 in pg_hba.conf and reload. Find users still on MD5 with:

SELECT rolname FROM pg_authid WHERE rolpassword LIKE 'md5%';

docs.title: Steps to Allow a Remote Client
docs.text:
1. Back up pg_hba.conf and postgresql.conf.
  2. In postgresql.conf, set listen_addresses = '*' (or a specific server IP). This change requires a restart.
  3. In pg_hba.conf, add a line for the client, for example host all all 192.168.4.25/32 scram-sha-256.
  4. Restart PostgreSQL if listen_addresses changed; otherwise a reload is enough.
  5. Check the file for errors:
SELECT rule_number, file_name, line_number, type, database, user_name,
       address, auth_method, error
FROM pg_hba_file_rules;
  1. Connect from the client:
psql -h <server_host> -U postgres -d postgres

Depending on the authentication method, the client may or may not be prompted for a password.

docs.title: Creating a Database
docs.text:
• A database is an organised collection of structured data.
  • The PostgreSQL bin folder contains command-line utilities that can run database tasks without opening psql, for example createdb, dropdb, createuser and dropuser.
  • The same tasks can be done with SQL from psql.

From psql:

CREATE DATABASE samson OWNER postgres;

From the command line:

createdb -O postgres -U postgres samson
createdb --help

  • \l or \l+ in psql lists all databases.
  • The pg_database catalog also holds database information.

docs.title: Dropping a Database
docs.text:
• You cannot drop the database you are connected to.
  • Only a superuser or the database owner can drop a database.
scott=# DROP DATABASE nano;
ERROR:  cannot drop the currently open database

From psql (connected to a different database):

DROP DATABASE nano;

From the command line:

dropdb nano
dropdb --help

docs.title: Creating Users
docs.text:
• Database users (roles) are completely separate from operating system users.
  • User names must be unique; names starting with pg_ are reserved.
  • The postgres superuser is created during installation and has all privileges.
  • Only a superuser or a role with the CREATEROLE attribute can create users. Since PostgreSQL 16, a CREATEROLE user can only manage roles it has ADMIN OPTION on (by default, the roles it created itself), and cannot grant attributes it does not have.
  • Roles are global to the cluster: one role can connect to any database in the instance, subject to pg_hba.conf and the CONNECT privilege.
  • CREATE USER is the same as CREATE ROLE with the LOGIN attribute.

From psql (creates superuser scott):

CREATE USER scott WITH LOGIN SUPERUSER PASSWORD 'scott';

From the command line:

createuser -U postgres -P -S scott

Option Meaning -U User name to connect as (not the user being created) -P Prompt for a password for the new role -S The new role is not a superuser (default) scott The role to create

Interactive mode:

$ createuser --interactive joe
Shall the new role be a superuser? (y/n) n
Shall the new role be allowed to create databases? (y/n) y
Shall the new role be allowed to create more new roles? (y/n) y

Use createuser --help for all options.

docs.title: Dropping Users
docs.text:
DROP USER username;      -- from psql
