SELECT pg_is_in_recovery(), pg_last_wal_receive_lsn(), pg_last_wal_replay_lsn(),
       now() - pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp() AS replay_delay;
SELECT status, sender_host, last_msg_receipt_time FROM pg_stat_wal_receiver;

-- logical replication (subscriber)
SELECT subname, worker_type, received_lsn, latest_end_time FROM pg_stat_subscription;
SELECT subname, apply_error_count, sync_error_count FROM pg_stat_subscription_stats;

-- WAL archiving health
SELECT archived_count, last_archived_wal, last_archived_time,
       failed_count, last_failed_wal, last_failed_time
FROM pg_stat_archiver;

On an idle primary replay_delay on the standby grows even when nothing is wrong; compare LSNs instead. Drop a slot you no longer need with SELECT pg_drop_replication_slot('name');.

docs.title: 10. Configuration checks
docs.text:
-- everything changed from the default, and where it was set
SELECT name, setting, unit, source, sourcefile
FROM pg_settings WHERE source NOT IN ('default', 'override') ORDER BY name;

-- changes waiting for a restart
SELECT name, setting FROM pg_settings WHERE pending_restart;

-- typos in postgresql.conf / pg_hba.conf (check before reload)
SELECT sourcefile, sourceline, name, error FROM pg_file_settings WHERE error IS NOT NULL;
SELECT line_number, error FROM pg_hba_file_rules WHERE error IS NOT NULL;

-- what a wait event means (v17)
SELECT type, name, description FROM pg_wait_events WHERE name = 'DataFileRead';

docs.title: 11. Taking action
docs.text:
SELECT pg_cancel_backend(12345);      -- stop the running query, keep the session
SELECT pg_terminate_backend(12345);   -- end the session (rolls back its transaction)

-- end sessions idle in a transaction for more than 15 minutes
SELECT pid, usename, pg_terminate_backend(pid)
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE state IN ('idle in transaction', 'idle in transaction (aborted)')
  AND state_change < now() - interval '15 minutes'
  AND pid <> pg_backend_pid();

-- end every other session on one database (e.g. before DROP or restore)
SELECT pg_terminate_backend(pid) FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE datname = 'shop' AND pid <> pg_backend_pid() AND backend_type = 'client backend';

VACUUM (VERBOSE, ANALYZE) public.orders;
REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY public.orders_pkey;
CHECKPOINT;

Safer than killing sessions: set idle_in_transaction_session_timeout and, new in v17, transaction_timeout for application roles.

docs.title: Fixes made to the course queries
docs.text: Course query used Problem Use instead procpid in pg_cancel_backend / pg_terminate_backend Column renamed in 9.2 pid WHERE query != '<IDLE>' Idle sessions now report state WHERE state <> 'idle' WHERE waiting Column removed in 9.6 wait_event_type = 'Lock' or pg_blocking_pids() age(query_start, clock_timestamp()) Arguments reversed, gives negative runtime clock_timestamp() - query_start SELECT user, ... in the long-running query user is your own name, not the session's usename pg_stat_statements total_time, mean_time Renamed in v13 total_exec_time, mean_exec_time pg_stat_statements blk_read_time, blk_write_time Renamed in v17 shared_blk_read_time, shared_blk_write_time pg_stat_bgwriter checkpoints_timed, checkpoints_req, buffers_checkpoint, checkpoint_write_time Moved in v17 pg_stat_checkpointer num_timed, num_requested, buffers_written, write_time pg_stat_bgwriter buffers_backend, buffers_backend_fsync Removed in v17 pg_stat_io writes, fsyncs for backend_type 'client backend' pg_stat_progress_vacuum max_dead_tuples, num_dead_tuples Renamed in v17 max_dead_tuple_bytes, num_dead_item_ids pg_relation_size(relname::regclass) Fails for tables outside search_path or with mixed case pg_relation_size(relid) indexrelname::regclass Same problem for indexes indexrelid 100 * idx_scan / (seq_scan + idx_scan) Division by zero; integer maths 100.0 * idx_scan / nullif(seq_scan + idx_scan, 0) seq_scan / seq_tup_read AS seq_tup_avg Inverted, and integer division seq_tup_read / nullif(seq_scan, 0) Index cache ratio (hit - read) / hit Wrong formula hit / (hit + read) 'fillfactor=(d+)' in regexp_matches Missing backslash, never matches 'fillfactor=(\d+)' "All databases and their sizes" = SELECT * FROM pg_user Labels swapped with the next query Use the pg_database size query in section 1 Kill-all query without pid <> pg_backend_pid() Kills your own session too Always exclude your own pid old_snapshot_threshold Parameter removed in v17 Use idle_in_transaction_session_timeout / transaction_timeout pg_last_wal_receive__lsn, pg_stat_subcription, pg_stat_statments, checkpoints_reg, select * form Typos Spellings as above

docs.title: Other course statements corrected for PostgreSQL 17
docs.text: Course says Correct for v17 A table can't exceed 32 GB 32 TB (8 kB blocks) checkpoint_timeout default is 10 min in v16 Still 5 min in 16 and 17 log_rotation_age = 1440 is seven days 1440 minutes is one day; seven days comes from %a in log_filename + truncate on rotation log_temp_files / log_filename need a restart A reload is enough (logging_collector does need a restart) Default log directory pg_log, WAL directory pg_xlog log and pg_wal since v10 checkpoint_segments Replaced by max_wal_size / min_wal_size in 9.5 Stats collector process Removed in v15; statistics live in shared memory autovacuum memory is capped at 1 GB Cap removed in v17; dead-row storage is far more compact Wraparound: database goes read-only at 4 billion The limit is about 2.1 billion (2^31); writes are refused about 3 million XIDs before it VACUUM (VERBOSE, ANALYZE) does not freeze Every VACUUM freezes rows older than vacuum_freeze_min_age; FREEZE does it for all Exceeding max_connections gives "out of memory" FATAL: sorry, too many clients already Heap fetches happen because someone changed the page Pages not marked all-visible in the visibility map; VACUUM sets the bit NULLs sort first in a B-tree; use hash indexes for NULL-heavy columns ASC indexes store NULLs last; hash indexes don't index NULLs at all GIN for range types GiST / SP-GiST for ranges Expression indexes can use max/min/count Only IMMUTABLE functions and operators, never aggregates ANALYZE TABLE t ANALYZE t pg_total_index_size() Doesn't exist; use pg_indexes_size(table) Hash join is fastest for any big join; LIMIT reads the whole table Depends on input sizes and memory; Limit stops early unless a Sort or Aggregate is below it CTE rewrite makes the query faster CTEs are inlined since v12; the gain comes from aggregating before the join Sync or async can be chosen per table Per transaction, session or role via synchronous_commit Pgpool-II / HAProxy are PostgreSQL extensions They are separate middleware PostgreSQL alone handles only about 350 TPS That was connection-setup overhead without pooling, not a server limit "Three ways to promote" (trigger file) promote_trigger_file removed in v16: use pg_ctl promote or pg_promote() pg_start_backup / pg_stop_backup, pg_is_in_backup Removed in v15: pg_backup_start / pg_backup_stop origin = all Valid values are none and any pg_stat_subscription_status pg_stat_subscription_stats repmgr 5.2 (repmgr12) repmgr 5.5 (repmgr_17) for v17 md4 in pg_hba.conf; md5 recommended md4 is invalid; use scram-sha-256 (md5 deprecated) pgBadger CSV output, --format csv --format sets the input format; output is html, text, json or bin CentOS 7 / Debian 10 / PostgreSQL 12–14 packages in labs Use RHEL 8/9 or Debian 12 with postgresql17 packages

docs.title: Feature history 13 → 16
docs.text: The courses have a module per release (DB-1 Modules 18–19, the Tour of PostgreSQL 16, DB-2 Module 7). Everything listed here is still in 17 unless marked. Use it to know which features exist on older servers you still run.

docs.title: PostgreSQL 13 (September 2020)
docs.text: Feature Use B-tree deduplication Repeated key values stored once, so indexes are smaller and faster. Indexes carried over by pg_upgrade from ≤12 need REINDEX to benefit Incremental sort Reuses an existing sort order, e.g. index on c1 when sorting by c1, c2; great with LIMIT Parallel VACUUM of indexes VACUUM (PARALLEL 2, VERBOSE) t; governed by max_parallel_maintenance_workers and min_parallel_index_scan_size Insert-triggered autovacuum Append-only tables now get vacuumed (autovacuum_vacuum_insert_threshold / _scale_factor) Backup manifests pg_basebackup writes backup_manifest; check with pg_verifybackup EXPLAIN (WAL) WAL records and bytes per statement: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, WAL, COSTS OFF) UPDATE t1 SET id = 1 WHERE id = 1; DROP DATABASE ... WITH (FORCE) Disconnects users, then drops Trusted extensions Database owners can install e.g. pgcrypto, plperl, ltree without superuser New views pg_stat_progress_basebackup, pg_stat_progress_analyze, pg_shmem_allocations; leader_pid in pg_stat_activity wal_keep_size Replaced wal_keep_segments

docs.title: PostgreSQL 14 (September 2021)
docs.text: Feature Use Predefined roles pg_read_all_data / pg_write_all_data Read-only or read-write access to everything without per-table grants idle_session_timeout, client_connection_check_interval Clean up idle or vanished clients Faster connection scalability and snapshot handling Many more idle connections tolerated vacuum_failsafe_age, REINDEX ... CONCURRENTLY on partitioned tables Safer anti-wraparound vacuum, online partition reindexing pg_stat_wal, pg_stat_replication_slots WAL and logical slot statistics libpq target_session_attrs primary / standby / prefer-standby Finer client failover analyze_new_cluster.sh removed from pg_upgrade Use vacuumdb --all --analyze-in-stages

docs.title: PostgreSQL 15 (October 2022)
docs.text:
Feature Use MERGE One statement that conditionally inserts, updates or deletes; needs the matching DML privileges; not on materialized views or foreign tables (see example below) Statistics in shared memory Stats collector process removed; pg_stat_tmp no longer used. Check its memory with SELECT name, total_bytes FROM pg_backend_memory_contexts WHERE name LIKE 'PgStat%'; jsonlog log_destination = 'jsonlog' (with logging_collector) for structured logs; combine with stderr, csvlog, syslog Logical replication row filters, column lists, FOR TABLES IN SCHEMA Publish only part of a table or a whole schema ALTER SUBSCRIPTION ... SKIP, disable_on_error, pg_stat_subscription_stats Handle and monitor replication conflicts New roles: pg_checkpoint; GRANT ... ON PARAMETER Delegate CHECKPOINT and specific ALTER SYSTEM rights psql \dconfig Search settings: \dconfig *mem* UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT Treat NULLs as equal in unique constraints pg_basebackup server-side compression, lz4 and zstd pg_basebackup --compress=server-zstd:level=9,workers=2 -Ft -D back.2 Exclusive backup mode removed pg_start_backup / pg_stop_backup became pg_backup_start / pg_backup_stop; pg_is_in_backup removed VACUUM VERBOSE output Adds read rates, buffer use and WAL generated CREATE privilege on public schema revoked from PUBLIC New databases are more secure by default 
MERGE INTO customer_history c
USING daily_orders d ON c.customer_id = d.customer_id
WHEN MATCHED THEN
  UPDATE SET order_count = c.order_count + 1, last_order_id = d.order_id
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN
  INSERT (customer_id, last_order_id, order_center, order_count, last_order)
  VALUES (d.customer_id, d.order_id, d.order_center, 1, d.order_time);
-- v17 adds:  WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE THEN DELETE   and   RETURNING merge_action(), c.*

docs.title: PostgreSQL 16 (September 2023)
docs.text:
Feature Use pg_stat_io I/O by backend type (9 types), object (relation / temp relation) and context (normal, vacuum, bulkread, bulkwrite) with reads, writes, extends, hits, evictions, reuses, fsyncs. High evictions → shared_buffers too small. Reset: SELECT pg_stat_reset_shared('io'); Drawback: no per-database or per-table split Faster COPY Bulk loading up to 3× faster; course demo 15 M rows: ~12 s on 15, ~7 s on 16 Parallel FULL and RIGHT joins More queries can use Gather with parallel workers Incremental sort for SELECT DISTINCT Automatic auto_explain logs parameter values auto_explain.log_parameter_max_length shows the bind values of slow statements Regular expressions in pg_hba.conf / pg_ident.conf Match many databases or users with one line Logical replication from a standby, bidirectional (origin = none), binary initial copy, parallel apply, pg_create_subscription role See the replication section load_balance_hosts in libpq Spread connections across listed hosts reserved_connections, pg_use_reserved_connections Keep slots free for named roles vacuum_buffer_usage_limit, VACUUM (BUFFER_USAGE_LIMIT) Control the buffer ring size for VACUUM last_seq_scan / last_idx_scan columns When a table or index was last used, which helps find unused indexes

Auto-explain setup (from the v16 tour):

session_preload_libraries = 'auto_explain'     # or shared_preload_libraries
auto_explain.log_min_duration = '5s'
auto_explain.log_analyze = on
auto_explain.log_buffers = on
auto_explain.log_parameter_max_length = -1     # v16: log all bind parameter values

pg_stat_io reading guide: combine backend_type + object + context to read a row. For example, client backend + relation + normal + reads = ordinary query reads, and client backend + relation + bulkwrite + writes = COPY. extends = files growing; op_bytes = 8 KB block; hits = served from shared_buffers (want high); reuses = ring-buffer reuse during bulk operations; fsyncs = forced syncs (want near zero for client backends). Reset monthly and compare before and after configuration changes.

docs.title: PostgreSQL 17 notes
docs.text: PostgreSQL 17 (released September 2024) keeps the same architecture as 16, so everything in this guide applies. The changes below matter most for DBAs; the course material was written for 12–16, so watch for the renamed views and columns.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text: Change What it means for you New VACUUM memory structure (TID store) Uses up to 20× less memory and is no longer capped at 1 GB, so a larger maintenance_work_mem / autovacuum_work_mem now really helps big tables. Index passes are much rarer Streaming / combined I/O for sequential scans and ANALYZE Fewer, larger reads; tune with io_combine_limit (default 128 kB) Faster WAL writes under high concurrency Better commit throughput on busy OLTP systems B-tree IN (...) lists scanned more efficiently Faster multi-value lookups, no change needed Better planning for CTEs, IS NOT NULL on NOT NULL columns, correlated subqueries Some query rewrites from older courses are no longer needed; check with EXPLAIN EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, SERIALIZE, MEMORY) Shows time to send results to the client and planner memory use COPY ... (ON_ERROR ignore) Bulk loads skip bad rows instead of failing

docs.title: Monitoring changes (update your scripts)
docs.text: Before 17 In 17 pg_stat_bgwriter: checkpoints_timed, checkpoints_req, buffers_checkpoint, checkpoint_write_time, checkpoint_sync_time pg_stat_checkpointer: num_timed, num_requested, buffers_written, write_time, sync_time (plus restartpoint counters on standbys) pg_stat_bgwriter: buffers_backend, buffers_backend_fsync Removed; use pg_stat_io (backend_type = 'client backend') pg_stat_statements: blk_read_time, blk_write_time shared_blk_read_time, shared_blk_write_time, plus local_blk_* times; stats_since / minmax_stats_since show when counting started pg_stat_progress_vacuum: max_dead_tuples, num_dead_tuples max_dead_tuple_bytes, dead_tuple_bytes, num_dead_item_ids — pg_wait_events: description of every wait event — pg_replication_slots: inactive_since, failover, synced old_snapshot_threshold Removed

docs.title: Backup and recovery
docs.text:
Incremental backups with pg_basebackup (needs summarize_wal = on):

pg_basebackup -D /backup/full -c fast                                     # full backup
pg_basebackup -D /backup/incr1 --incremental=/backup/full/backup_manifest  # only changed blocks
pg_combinebackup /backup/full /backup/incr1 -o /restore/data              # rebuild a full data dir

This cuts backup time and space for large, mostly static databases. Also new: pg_walsummary to inspect WAL summaries.

docs.title: Replication and HA
docs.text:
• Failover slots: logical replication slots created with failover = true (and sync_replication_slots = on on the standby) are copied to the standby, so logical subscribers keep working after a failover.

  • pg_createsubscriber turns a physical standby into a logical subscriber without copying the data again.

  • pg_upgrade keeps logical replication slots and subscriptions when upgrading from 17 onward, so logical setups survive major upgrades.

docs.title: Administration and security
docs.text:
• transaction_timeout: ends any transaction (not just idle ones) that runs longer than the limit.

  • New predefined role pg_maintain: lets a role run VACUUM, ANALYZE, REINDEX, CLUSTER, REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW and LOCK TABLE without being the owner, which is good for maintenance accounts.

  • allow_alter_system = off blocks ALTER SYSTEM when configuration is managed by tools such as Ansible or Patroni.

  • SQL: MERGE ... RETURNING, MERGE on views, JSON_TABLE and other SQL/JSON functions.

  • Install packages are named postgresql17-server / postgresql17-contrib, with binaries in /usr/pgsql-17/bin and data in /var/lib/pgsql/17/data on RHEL.

docs.title: Upgrading to 17
docs.text:
1. Read the release notes for removed features (for example old_snapshot_threshold, db_user_namespace, the adminpack extension).

  2. Update monitoring scripts for the renamed views and columns above.

  3. Run pg_upgrade --check, then upgrade with --link or --clone.

  4. Run vacuumdb --all --analyze-in-stages, then ALTER EXTENSION pg_stat_statements UPDATE; in each database.

  5. Re-check your baseline (top SQL, cache hit ratio, checkpoints) before and after.

docs.title: Learning path checklist
docs.text:
Tick an item once you can do it on a test server without notes.

Beginner

  • [ ] Install PostgreSQL with contrib and connect with psql

  • [ ] Create a database, tables with keys and constraints, and load sample data

  • [ ] Write SELECT with WHERE, JOIN, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY, LIMIT

  • [ ] Use transactions (BEGIN, COMMIT, ROLLBACK) and \timing

Intermediate

  • [ ] Explain postmaster, backends, shared buffers, WAL and the background processes

  • [ ] Change a parameter with ALTER SYSTEM and know whether it needs reload or restart

  • [ ] Create roles, grant privileges and write pg_hba.conf rules

  • [ ] Take and restore pg_dump (custom, parallel, one table) and pg_basebackup backups

  • [ ] Set up WAL archiving and do a point-in-time recovery

Advanced DBA

  • [ ] Explain MVCC, dead rows, VACUUM vs VACUUM FULL, and XID wraparound

  • [ ] Build a declaratively partitioned table and drop an old partition

  • [ ] Set up a streaming standby, monitor lag, and promote it

  • [ ] Set up logical replication for selected tables

  • [ ] Run pg_upgrade with --check and --link

Performance tuning

  • [ ] Record a baseline with pg_stat_statements and pgbench

  • [ ] Size shared_buffers, effective_cache_size, work_mem and maintenance_work_mem for a given server

  • [ ] Tune checkpoints so most are timed; read pg_stat_bgwriter / pg_stat_checkpointer

  • [ ] Set random_page_cost and effective_io_concurrency for SSD storage

  • [ ] Tune autovacuum per table and find what blocks cleanup

  • [ ] Read EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) and spot bad row estimates, disk sorts and filter waste

  • [ ] Choose B-tree, GIN, BRIN, partial, expression and covering indexes; find missing and unused ones

  • [ ] Fix estimates with ANALYZE, SET STATISTICS and CREATE STATISTICS

  • [ ] Rewrite slow queries (sargable ranges, NOT EXISTS, keyset pagination, select only needed columns)

  • [ ] Diagnose waits and locks from pg_stat_activity

  • [ ] Configure logging, produce a pgBadger report, and set up PgBouncer

Operations, HA and upgrades

  • [ ] Run the daily diagnostic queries and explain each result

  • [ ] Restore a single table and a single schema from a custom-format dump; restore a database under a new name

  • [ ] Take full and incremental (v17) backups and combine them; verify with pg_verifybackup

  • [ ] Recover to a timestamp and to a named restore point

  • [ ] Build a log-shipping standby and a streaming standby with a slot; switch to synchronous mode

  • [ ] Set up repmgr with automatic failover, rejoin the old primary, add a witness, do a switchover

  • [ ] Rebuild an old primary with pg_rewind

  • [ ] Configure logical replication with a row filter, fix a conflict with SKIP, and set up bidirectional replication with origin = none

  • [ ] Put PgBouncer in front of an application and compare pgbench results

  • [ ] Upgrade a 16 cluster to 17 with pg_upgrade --link, including standbys and extensions, and know the rollback options

  • [ ] Produce a pg_profile report and a pgBadger report for the same day

Source material: the course folders under PostgreSQL\Study (DB-1, DB-2, Backup&Restore Fundamental, the HA and Scalability course, PostgreSQL-PT, High_Performance, Beginner sample data). Parameter defaults, view names and paths are for PostgreSQL 17.

docs.title: PostgreSQL Emergency Runbook: Resolving pg_wal Disk Space Exhaustion
docs.text: This runbook outlines the immediate diagnostics and mitigation steps when the PostgreSQL Write-Ahead Log (pg_wal) directory (formerly known as pg_xlog in PostgreSQL 9.6 and older) runs out of disk space, causing the database to crash and fail to start.

docs.title: 1. Symptoms of a Full pg_wal Directory
docs.text: When the storage partition hosting pg_wal becomes 100% full, the PostgreSQL engine cannot write new WAL records and will automatically trigger a panic shutdown to prevent data corruption.

docs.title: Connection Failure Messages (When attempting to reconnect):
docs.text:
psql: could not connect to server: No such file or directory
  Is the server running locally and accepting connections on Unix domain socket "/var/run/postgresql/.s.PGSQL.5432"?

docs.title: PostgreSQL System Log Messages (Critical Indicators):
docs.text:
LOG: archiver process (PID 4103) exited with exit code 1
PANIC: could not write to file "pg_wal/waltemp.4111": No space left on device
LOG: server process (PID 4111) was terminated by signal 6: Aborted
FATAL: the database system is in recovery mode
LOG: database system was not properly shut down; automatic recovery in progress
LOG: redo starts at 29/8D242168
PANIC: could not write to file "pg_wal/waltemp.4920": No space left on device
LOG: startup process (PID 4920) was terminated by signal 6: Aborted
LOG: aborting startup due to startup process failure

docs.title: 2. Most Common Causes of pg_wal Accumulation
docs.text: PostgreSQL accumulates pg_wal files when write-ahead log generation outpaces the database's ability to recycle or delete them. The most common causes are:

docs.title: Replication Bottlenecks
docs.text:
• Stalled Replication Slots: A standby server or a CDC tool (like Debezium) drops offline, but the replication slot remains active on the primary database. PostgreSQL will indefinitely retain all new WAL segments generated since the consumer went offline, waiting for it to reconnect and catch up.
  • Replication Lag: High network latency, heavy read traffic bottlenecks on hot standbys, or underpowered replica hardware can cause the standby to fall too far behind the primary, delaying WAL recycling.
  • Excessive wal_keep_size: Setting this parameter (or the older wal_keep_segments) too high forces the primary server to retain large amounts of WAL history for non-slot replicas, even if they are caught up.

docs.title: Archiving and Maintenance Failures
docs.text:
• Failing archive_command: If external archiving scripts fail (due to incorrect paths, network/VPN issues, or target storage exhaustion), Postgres blocks WAL deletion/recycling until files are safely archived.
  • Infrequent Checkpoints: High checkpoint_timeout settings or large max_wal_size configurations cause PostgreSQL to wait longer before triggering checkpoints and recycling older WAL blocks.

docs.title: Workload Spikes
docs.text:
• Heavy Write Activity: Massive data loads, bulk inserts, or unoptimized batch jobs generate gigabytes of logs faster than background writers can process and clean them.
  • full_page_writes Overhead: Heavy updates immediately following a checkpoint force Postgres to write full disk pages to the WAL, causing rapid volume expansion.

docs.title: 3. Troubleshooting & Resolution Steps (Reactive)
docs.text:
If your database has crashed and refuses to start due to a full disk, choose the most appropriate resolution strategy below.

[!CAUTION] NEVER delete active WAL files directly using rm. Deleting arbitrary WAL files will cause data inconsistency and make the database unrecoverable. Follow the validated methods below.

docs.title: Method A: Resolve WAL Archiving Failures (If Applicable)
docs.text: If WAL archiving (archive_mode = on) is configured, PostgreSQL will not remove or recycle WAL segments from pg_wal until they are successfully processed by the archive_command. If archiving fails or lags behind, WAL files will pile up indefinitely.

docs.title: 1. Identify the Archiving Issue
docs.text:
Review the recent PostgreSQL log files for failed archive commands: 

LOG: archive command failed with exit code 1
DETAIL: The failed archive command was: gzip < pg_wal/0000000400000028000000CD > /archive/arc/0000000400000028000000CD

docs.title: 2. Troubleshoot and Fix
docs.text:
• Check if the destination archive directory has run out of space.
  • Verify that the postgres system user has proper write permissions on the archive path.
  • Ensure the target mount point is active and accessible.

docs.title: 3. Start the Database
docs.text:
Once the archiving path or command issue is fixed, start the PostgreSQL service: 

pg_ctl start -D /path/to/pg_data
The database will recover, process the archived WAL logs, and automatically delete/recycle the obsolete files, reclaiming disk space.

docs.title: Method B: Temporary Relocation of pg_wal (Symlinking)
docs.text: If you cannot add space to the partition immediately, you can move the entire WAL directory to a separate partition that has free space.

docs.title: 1. Restrict Connections (Maintenance Mode)
docs.text:
Modify pg_hba.conf temporarily to prevent application connections while database maintenance is in progress: 

# Temporarily reject or restrict user connections
local   all             all                                     reject
host    all             all             0.0.0.0/0               reject

docs.title: 2. Copy the WAL logs to the new location
docs.text:
Create a new directory on a partition with sufficient free space and copy the contents of pg_wal to it: 

cp -rf /database/pgdata/pg_wal/* /mnt/new_disk/postgres/pg_wal/

docs.title: 3. Backup and Remove the Original Directory
docs.text:
Rename the original directory: 

mv /database/pgdata/pg_wal /database/pgdata/pg_wal_bkp

docs.title: 4. Create the Symbolic Link
docs.text:
Create a symlink in the data directory pointing to the new WAL location: 

ln -s /mnt/new_disk/postgres/pg_wal/ /database/pgdata/pg_wal

docs.title: 5. Start the Database & Verify
docs.text:
Start the database service and verify that new WAL logs are being created in the new location: 

pg_ctl start -D /database/pgdata
If PostgreSQL starts successfully and runs without errors, you can safely delete the backup: 
rm -rf /database/pgdata/pg_wal_bkp

docs.title: 6. Revert Maintenance Mode
docs.text: Restore the original rules in pg_hba.conf and reload the configuration.

docs.title: Method C: Delete the Emergency Dummy File
docs.text: If you previously followed proactive guidelines and pre-allocated an emergency space-reserve dummy file inside pg_wal (or on the same mount point), you can delete it to quickly reclaim space, start the database, and trigger a cleanup checkpoint.

docs.title: 1. Delete the Reserve File
docs.text: rm /database/pgdata/pg_wal/ONLY_DELETE_THIS_DUMMY_FILE_IN_A_POSTGRES_EMERGENCY

docs.title: 2. Start PostgreSQL
docs.text: pg_ctl start -D /database/pgdata

docs.title: 3. Run a Checkpoint
docs.text:
Connect to the database and trigger a checkpoint to force PostgreSQL to immediately recycle unused WAL segments and free up space: 

psql -d postgres -c "CHECKPOINT;"

docs.title: How to Configure Method C (Pre-allocation in Healthy State)
docs.text:
To configure this safeguard during a healthy database state (or to recreate it after recovering from an emergency), execute the following commands as the postgres user:

# Navigate to the pg_wal directory
cd /database/pgdata/pg_wal

# Pre-allocate a 300MB reserve file (block size 1MB, count 300)
dd if=/dev/zero of=ONLY_DELETE_THIS_DUMMY_FILE_IN_A_POSTGRES_EMERGENCY bs=1M count=300

This pre-allocates contiguous physical blocks on disk. If the database volume hits 100% usage and PostgreSQL halts, deleting this file instantly frees up 300MB of space, providing enough headroom for PostgreSQL to boot up and run a checkpoint to clean up the actual WAL files.

docs.title: Method D: Safe Manual WAL Cleanup using pg_archivecleanup
docs.text: If you cannot start the database to perform a checkpoint, you must find which WAL files are older than the active checkpoint and delete only those.

docs.title: 1. Identify the Latest Checkpoint REDO WAL File
docs.text:
Execute pg_controldata pointing to your data directory and locate the REDO WAL file name: 

pg_controldata -D /database/pgdata
Look for this line in the output: 
Latest checkpoint's REDO WAL file:   000000010000000F00000026

docs.title: 2. Run a Dry Run of the Cleanup
docs.text:
Use pg_archivecleanup with the -n flag to preview which files are older than the REDO WAL file and will be safely deleted: 

pg_archivecleanup -n /database/pgdata/pg_wal 000000010000000F00000026

docs.title: 3. Perform the Deletion
docs.text:
Once verified, execute the command with the -d (delete) flag to clean up the files: 

pg_archivecleanup -d /database/pgdata/pg_wal 000000010000000F00000026

docs.title: 4. Start the Database and Take a Backup
docs.text: Start the PostgreSQL server. Once running, take a fresh cluster backup immediately to establish a clean recovery baseline.

docs.title: 4. Proactive Best Practices
docs.text: To prevent pg_wal exhaustion in production, implement the following guardrails:

docs.title: 1. Monitor Disk Space and Alert Early
docs.text: Set up disk usage monitoring for the PostgreSQL partitions. Configure email/SMS alerts to fire when disk usage hits 70% (Warning) and 90% (Critical).

docs.title: 2. Compress Archived WAL Logs
docs.text:
Reduce archive storage requirements by compressing WAL files inside your archive_command: 

archive_command = 'gzip < %p > /archive_dir/%f'
Note: If you compress files, your restore_command during recovery must decompress them: 
restore_command = 'gunzip < /archive_dir/%f > %p'

docs.title: 3. Pre-Allocate an Emergency Space-Reserve File
docs.text:
Create a 300MB (or larger) dummy file in the pg_wal directory. This file does not serve any transactional purpose but acts as a space buffer that can be deleted to recover from a disk full shutdown scenario: 

dd if=/dev/zero of=/database/pgdata/pg_wal/ONLY_DELETE_THIS_DUMMY_FILE_IN_A_POSTGRES_EMERGENCY bs=1MB count=300

docs.title: PostgreSQL AutoTune: Azure VM Scale Implementation
docs.text:
Version 4.0 - Systemd ExecStartPre Architecture

  • Script: pg_autotune_systemd.sh → Deploy to /u01/Gsl/pg_autotune_systemd.sh
  • Log Directory: /u01/backup/logs/autotune/

docs.title: 1. Overview
docs.text:
This document describes the design, workflow, and implementation of the Version 4 PostgreSQL Auto-Tuning solution for self-hosted PostgreSQL 16/17 on Azure Linux VMs (RHEL 8). When an Azure VM is scaled up or down, the script automatically detects the new hardware profile and applies optimized PostgreSQL parameters on startup - with zero manual intervention and zero double restarts.

The memory allocation formulas calculate shared_buffers at 26% and effective_cache_size at 76% of OS-visible physical RAM (MemTotal). It also uses the dynamically detected PG_VERSION for service restarts. In V4, the email functionality has been entirely removed to focus on reliable log tracing, and the CPU fallback formula for max_parallel_workers_per_gather was updated.

docs.title: 2.1 Visual Execution Flow
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    VMStart["VM Boots / systemctl start"] --> Systemd["Systemd prepares to start PostgreSQL"]
    Systemd --> ExecStartPre["Execute ExecStartPre Hook as root (+ prefix)"]
    ExecStartPre --> InitLogging["Initialize Log File in /u01/backup/logs/autotune/"]
    InitLogging --> LocatePGData{"Is $PGDATA set & postgresql.conf present?"}

    LocatePGData -- Yes --> SetConfPath["Set PG_CONF and PGDATA_DIR"]
    LocatePGData -- No --> FallbackPGData["Read PGDATA via su - postgres"]

    FallbackPGData --> LocatePGDataFallback{"Did fallback find PGDATA?"}
    LocatePGDataFallback -- Yes --> SetConfPath
    LocatePGDataFallback -- No --> ExitError["Exit 1 with Critical Error (Blocks startup)"]

    SetConfPath --> DetectVersion["Detect PG_VERSION via postgres -V binary"]
    DetectVersion --> DetectHardware["Detect RAM from /proc/meminfo & CPU from nproc"]
    DetectHardware --> ConstructState["Build CURRENT_STATE spec string"]

    ConstructState --> CheckState{"CURRENT_STATE == LAST_KNOWN_STATE?"}
    CheckState -- Yes --> ExitSuccess["Hardware unchanged: Exit 0 (No changes)"]
    CheckState -- No --> LogHardwareBlock["Log HARDWARE CHANGE DETECTED details"]

    LogHardwareBlock --> CalcMem["Calculate Memory Params: 26% shared, 76% cache, 5% maint"]
    CalcMem --> CallAPI["Call pgconfig.org API (5s timeout)"]

    CallAPI --> CheckAPI{"Did API return CPU parameters?"}
    CheckAPI -- Yes --> ParseAPI["Parse CPU params from API response"]
    CheckAPI -- No --> LocalCPUFallback["Apply local CPU fallback: min(4, CPU/2)"]

    ParseAPI --> Backup["Backup postgresql.conf with timestamp"]
    LocalCPUFallback --> Backup

    Backup --> ApplyParams["Apply 8 parameters via sed & log changes"]
    ApplyParams --> UpdateState["Rewrite LAST_KNOWN_STATE inside script file"]
    UpdateState --> TestSleep{"TEST_SLEEP_SECONDS > 0?"}

    TestSleep -- Yes --> ExecSleep["Sleep N seconds for testing"]
    TestSleep -- No --> ScriptExit

    ExecSleep --> ScriptExit["Script Exits 0"]
    ScriptExit --> NativeStart["Systemd ExecStart: PostgreSQL starts natively"]
    ExitSuccess --> NativeStart

docs.title: 2.2 Step-by-Step Logic
docs.text:
1. Logging Initialization: Redirects stdout and stderr into /u01/backup/logs/autotune/pg_autotune_[TIMESTAMP].log.
  2. Configuration Discovery: Locates postgresql.conf using $PGDATA or falls back to querying the postgres user profile environment.
  3. Version & Hardware Detection: Checks the version by running postgres -V and reads CPU cores (nproc) and memory (/proc/meminfo).
  4. State Validation: Compares the new hardware profile string against the LAST_KNOWN_STATE stored in the script. If they match, the script exits silently (exit 0).
  5. Memory & CPU Tuning: If hardware changed, memory params are calculated locally. CPU parallel params are fetched from pgconfig.org API with a local fallback of min(4, CPU_CORES/2) if offline.
  6. State Save & Boot: Backs up postgresql.conf, applies changes via sed, updates its own LAST_KNOWN_STATE variable, and hands control back to Systemd.

docs.title: 3. V4 Memory and CPU Formulas
docs.text: Parameter Formula / Source Type 64 GB RAM, 16 CPU Example shared_buffers (RAM_MB * 26) / 100 Calculated 17039 MB (~16.6 GB) effective_cache_size (RAM_MB * 76) / 100 Calculated 49807 MB (~48.6 GB) maintenance_work_mem max(RAM_GB / 20, 1) * 1024 MB Calculated 3072 MB (3 GB) work_mem Static: WORK_MEM_MB User config 500 MB wal_buffers Static: WAL_BUFFERS_MB User config 32 MB max_worker_processes API or CPU_CORES API/Fallback 16 max_parallel_workers API or CPU_CORES API/Fallback 16 max_parallel_workers_per_gather API or min(4, CPU/2) API/Fallback 4

docs.title: Step 1: Place the Script
docs.text:
Copy pg_autotune_systemd.sh to /u01/Gsl/pg_autotune_systemd.sh and make it executable: 

cp pg_autotune_systemd.sh /u01/Gsl/pg_autotune_systemd.sh
sudo chmod +x /u01/Gsl/pg_autotune_systemd.sh

docs.title: Step 2: Configure Script Variables
docs.text:
Edit the USER CONFIGURATION block in the script to match your environment: 

MAX_CONNECTIONS=5000               # Passed to pgconfig.org API
WORK_MEM_MB=500                    # Static work_mem (MB)
WAL_BUFFERS_MB=32                  # Static wal_buffers (MB)
TEST_SLEEP_SECONDS=0               # Set to 0 for production!

docs.title: Step 3: Create Log Directories
docs.text: sudo mkdir -p /u01/backup/logs/autotune/config_backup

docs.title: Step 4: Configure SELinux Context (CRITICAL)
docs.text:
Systemd will block scripts in /u01/ from starting unless they carry the official bin_t context: 

sudo chcon -t bin_t /u01/Gsl/pg_autotune_systemd.sh

# Verify context:
ls -Z /u01/Gsl/pg_autotune_systemd.sh
# output should contain bin_t

docs.title: Step 5: Edit the Systemd unit file
docs.text:
Open the PostgreSQL unit file (e.g., /usr/lib/systemd/system/postgresql-16.service or postgresql-17.service) and insert the hook below [Service]: 

[Service]
ExecStartPre=+/u01/Gsl/pg_autotune_systemd.sh

[!IMPORTANT] The + prefix is mandatory. It grants root privileges to the script during execution.

docs.title: Step 6: Reload & Test
docs.text:
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl stop postgresql-16
sudo systemctl start postgresql-16

# Verify logs:
cat /u01/backup/logs/autotune/pg_autotune_*.log

docs.title: 5. Troubleshooting & Verification
docs.text:
• Verify active PG settings: 
    SHOW shared_buffers;
SHOW effective_cache_size;
  • SELinux execution block: If PostgreSQL fails to start, verify context using ls -Z /u01/Gsl/pg_autotune_systemd.sh and ensure the + prefix is added in the systemd service file.

docs.title: 6. Tuning Script Source Code
docs.text:
#!/bin/bash
# pg_autotune_systemd.sh — Version 4
# Detects hardware changes, modifies postgresql.conf.
# Designed exclusively to be run via Systemd ExecStartPre hook.
#
# V4 Changes:
#   - max_parallel_workers_per_gather fallback formula updated to: min(4, CPU/2)
#   - Email functionality removed entirely
# V3 Changes from V2:
#   - shared_buffers      : 25% → 26% of RAM
#   - effective_cache_size: 75% → 76% of RAM
#   - systemctl log message now uses dynamic PG_VERSION (no hardcoded '16')

# --- USER CONFIGURATION ---
MAX_CONNECTIONS=5000
WORK_MEM_MB=500
WAL_BUFFERS_MB=32
TEST_SLEEP_SECONDS=30
# --------------------------

# --- LOGGING CONFIGURATION ---
LOG_DIR="/u01/backup/logs/autotune"
LOG_FILE="${LOG_DIR}/pg_autotune_$(date +'%Y%m%d_%H%M%S').log"

# Auto-create log directory if it does not exist
if [ ! -d "$LOG_DIR" ]; then
    mkdir -p "$LOG_DIR" 2>/dev/null
fi

# Redirect all output to the log file
exec >> "$LOG_FILE" 2>&1

# Verify the log file was actually created (exec fails silently if dir is unwritable)
if [ ! -f "$LOG_FILE" ]; then
    # Fall back to stderr — visible via: journalctl -u postgresql-PG_VERSION
    exec >&2
    echo "[$(date '+%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S')] CRITICAL: Cannot write to log file: $LOG_FILE"
    echo "[$(date '+%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S')] CRITICAL: Check that $LOG_DIR exists and is writable by root."
    echo "[$(date '+%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S')] CRITICAL: Continuing — all output will appear in journalctl."
fi

log() {
    echo "[$(date '+%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S')] $*"
}

log "================================================================="
log "Executing PostgreSQL Auto-Tune Hook  (v4)"
# -----------------------------

# --- INTERNAL STATE (Do not modify manually) ---
LAST_KNOWN_STATE="First Run"
# -----------------------------------------------

# 1. Dynamically Locate postgresql.conf
log "Locating postgresql.conf dynamically using PGDATA..."

# Check if PGDATA is available in the current environment
if [ -n "$PGDATA" ] && [ -f "$PGDATA/postgresql.conf" ]; then
    PG_CONF="$PGDATA/postgresql.conf"
    PGDATA_DIR="$PGDATA"
else
    # Attempt to load the postgres user's environment variables (useful if running from root crontab)
    PGDATA_ENV=$(su - postgres -c 'echo $PGDATA' 2>/dev/null | grep -v '^\s*$' | tail -n 1)
    if [ -n "$PGDATA_ENV" ] && [ -f "$PGDATA_ENV/postgresql.conf" ]; then
        PG_CONF="$PGDATA_ENV/postgresql.conf"
        PGDATA_DIR="$PGDATA_ENV"
    else
        log "CRITICAL: \$PGDATA environment variable is not set or postgresql.conf not found inside it."
        log "Please ensure \$PGDATA is exported, or set PG_CONF manually."
        exit 1
    fi
fi
log "Found PostgreSQL Configuration: $PG_CONF"

# Dynamically Detect PostgreSQL Version
# Note: postgres -V reads the installed binary — does NOT require the service to be running.
PG_VERSION=$(postgres -V 2>/dev/null | awk '{print $NF}' | cut -d. -f1)
if [ -z "$PG_VERSION" ]; then
    PG_VERSION=$(psql -V 2>/dev/null | awk '{print $3}' | cut -d. -f1)
fi
if [ -z "$PG_VERSION" ]; then
    PG_VERSION="17" # Fallback
fi
log "Detected PostgreSQL Version: $PG_VERSION"

# 2. Detect Hardware
TOTAL_RAM_KB=$(grep MemTotal /proc/meminfo | awk '{print $2}')
TOTAL_RAM_MB=$((TOTAL_RAM_KB / 1024))
TOTAL_RAM_GB=$((TOTAL_RAM_MB / 1024))
CPU_CORES=$(nproc)

log "Detected Hardware: ${TOTAL_RAM_MB}MB RAM  |  ${CPU_CORES} CPU Cores"

CURRENT_STATE="${TOTAL_RAM_MB}MB_RAM-${CPU_CORES}_CPUS"

# 3. Hardware Change Validation (Self-contained)
if [ "$CURRENT_STATE" == "$LAST_KNOWN_STATE" ]; then
    log "Hardware unchanged ($CURRENT_STATE). Skipping auto-tune process."
    exit 0
fi

log "================================================================="
log "HARDWARE CHANGE DETECTED!"
log "Previous Hardware: $LAST_KNOWN_STATE"
log "New Hardware:      $CURRENT_STATE"
log "================================================================="

# 4. Memory Parameters (Local Math)
# shared_buffers      = 26% of OS-visible physical RAM (MemTotal)
# effective_cache_size= 76% of OS-visible physical RAM (MemTotal)  [planner hint only]
# maintenance_work_mem= 5% of RAM (RAM_GB / 20), minimum 1 GB
SHARED_BUFFERS_MB=$(( (TOTAL_RAM_MB * 26) / 100 ))
EFFECTIVE_CACHE_MB=$(( (TOTAL_RAM_MB * 76) / 100 ))

MAINT_WORK_MEM_GB=$((TOTAL_RAM_GB / 20))
if [ "$MAINT_WORK_MEM_GB" -lt 1 ]; then MAINT_WORK_MEM_GB=1; fi
MAINT_WORK_MEM_MB=$((MAINT_WORK_MEM_GB * 1024))

# work_mem and wal_buffers are static — set via USER CONFIGURATION block above

# 5. CPU/Parallel Parameters (API with Local Fallback)
API_URL="https://api.pgconfig.org/v1/tuning/get-config?format=conf&max_connections=${MAX_CONNECTIONS}&pg_version=${PG_VERSION}&environment_name=OLTP&total_ram=${TOTAL_RAM_GB}&cpus=${CPU_CORES}&drive_type=SSD&arch=x86-64&os_type=linux"
log "Calling pgconfig.org API for CPU/parallel parameters..."
API_CONF=$(curl -s --max-time 5 "$API_URL" 2>/dev/null)

if [ -n "$API_CONF" ] && echo "$API_CONF" | grep -q "max_parallel_workers"; then
    log "API call succeeded. Parsing CPU parameters from response."
    MAX_WORKER_PROCESSES=$(echo "$API_CONF" | grep "^max_worker_processes" | awk '{print $3}')
    MAX_PARALLEL_WORKERS=$(echo "$API_CONF" | grep "^max_parallel_workers " | awk '{print $3}')
    MAX_PARALLEL_WORKERS_PER_GATHER=$(echo "$API_CONF" | grep "^max_parallel_workers_per_gather" | awk '{print $3}')
else
    log "API call failed or timed out. Using local fallback math for CPU parameters."
    MAX_WORKER_PROCESSES=$CPU_CORES
    MAX_PARALLEL_WORKERS=$CPU_CORES
    # Formula: min(4, Total CPU Cores / 2)
    MAX_PARALLEL_WORKERS_PER_GATHER=$(( (CPU_CORES / 2) < 4 ? (CPU_CORES / 2) : 4 ))
    if [ "$MAX_PARALLEL_WORKERS_PER_GATHER" -eq 0 ]; then MAX_PARALLEL_WORKERS_PER_GATHER=1; fi
fi

# 6. Backup the Configuration
TIMESTAMP=$(date +"%Y%m%d_%H%M%S")
BACKUP_PATH="/u01/backup/logs/autotune/config_backup/postgresql.conf.backup.${TIMESTAMP}"
cp "$PG_CONF" "$BACKUP_PATH"
log "Backed up $PG_CONF to $BACKUP_PATH"

# 7. Direct File Modification Function
# Logs a before-and-after trace for every parameter change.
set_pg_param() {
    local key=$1
    local val=$2
    local prev_val
    if grep -qE "^\s*#?\s*${key}\s*=" "$PG_CONF"; then
        prev_val=$(grep -E "^\s*#?\s*${key}\s*=" "$PG_CONF" | head -n 1)
        sed -i -E "s/^\s*#?\s*${key}\s*=.*/${key} = ${val}/g" "$PG_CONF"
        log "Updated parameter:  [${prev_val}]   --->   [${key} = ${val}]"
    else
        echo "${key} = ${val}" >> "$PG_CONF"
        log "Added NEW parameter:   [${key} = ${val}]"
    fi
}

# Apply parameters
log "Applying optimized configurations to postgresql.conf..."
set_pg_param "shared_buffers"               "'${SHARED_BUFFERS_MB}MB'"
set_pg_param "effective_cache_size"         "'${EFFECTIVE_CACHE_MB}MB'"
set_pg_param "maintenance_work_mem"         "'${MAINT_WORK_MEM_MB}MB'"
set_pg_param "work_mem"                     "'${WORK_MEM_MB}MB'"
set_pg_param "wal_buffers"                  "'${WAL_BUFFERS_MB}MB'"
set_pg_param "max_worker_processes"         "$MAX_WORKER_PROCESSES"
set_pg_param "max_parallel_workers"         "$MAX_PARALLEL_WORKERS"
set_pg_param "max_parallel_workers_per_gather" "$MAX_PARALLEL_WORKERS_PER_GATHER"

# 8. (Restart logic removed - handled natively by systemd)

# 9. Update Self-Contained State
SCRIPT_PATH=$(readlink -f "$0")
sed -i -E "s/^LAST_KNOWN_STATE=.*/LAST_KNOWN_STATE=\"$CURRENT_STATE\"/" "$SCRIPT_PATH"
log "Process complete. State saved inside script."

# 10. Testing Gap (set TEST_SLEEP_SECONDS=0 in production)
if [ "$TEST_SLEEP_SECONDS" -gt 0 ]; then
    log "TESTING MODE: Sleeping for ${TEST_SLEEP_SECONDS} seconds to demonstrate ExecStartPre gap."
    log "You can check 'systemctl status postgresql-${PG_VERSION}' in another terminal now."
    log "The database engine will not start until this sleep finishes."
    sleep "$TEST_SLEEP_SECONDS"
    log "Sleep finished. Handing control back to systemd native auto-startup..."
fi

docs.title: PostgreSQL 16 Extension Compile Guide for RHEL 8
docs.text: Target OS: Red Hat Enterprise Linux 8 / AlmaLinux 8 / Rocky Linux 8 PostgreSQL Version: 16 Extension: pg_proctab (or similar PGXS-based extensions built from source)

docs.title: 1. Do I need to install it in every single database?
docs.text:
Yes. In PostgreSQL, extensions are installed on a strictly per-database basis. The extension's functions will only be queryable inside the specific databases where you have executed CREATE EXTENSION;.

Pro-Tip for Future Databases: If you want the extension to be automatically available in every brand new database you create in the future, you should install it into the template1 database. PostgreSQL uses template1 as the default blueprint for all new databases.

docs.title: 2. Portability & Compilation Environment Notes
docs.text:
[!IMPORTANT] OS & Architecture Dependency: Compiling extensions generates dynamic library files (.so binaries). These binaries are strictly compiled for the specific compiler version, OS kernel version, and CPU architecture of the host machine. Consequently, they are strictly OS-dependent. For example, you cannot copy a .so binary compiled on RHEL 8 to an instance running on Ubuntu or another incompatible OS.

[!TIP] Using a Development/Build Server: If you are compiling the extension on a Development/Build server to avoid installing compiler tools (like gcc, make, and development headers) on the live production server: 1. The Development/Build server must run the exact same OS distribution, version, architecture, and PostgreSQL version as the Production server. 2. Once successfully built, copy the compiled files from the Dev server to the Production server at the exact same paths: - Shared library file (.so): to /usr/pgsql-16/lib/ - Control (.control) and SQL (.sql) files: to /usr/pgsql-16/share/extension/

[!NOTE] Example Extension Only: The step-by-step commands below use the pg_proctab extension as a reference example. If you are building a different extension, you must substitute the download URLs, directory names, makefile patches (if any), SQL/extension names, and any extension-specific prerequisite packages/libraries with your own extension's source code and requirements.

docs.title: 3. End-to-End Compile and Install Steps
docs.text: We use the example of pg_proctab below, but this workflow applies to any PGXS-supported extension.

docs.title: Step 1: Install Development Tools (Only on Compilation/Build Host)
docs.text:
Install compiler tools and the specific PostgreSQL 16 development headers needed to build the extension. (If you are using a development/build server, run this step on that server only.) 

sudo dnf install -y gcc make postgresql16-devel redhat-rpm-config wget unzip

docs.title: Step 2: Download & Extract Source Code
docs.text:
cd /tmp
wget https://github.com/markwkm/pg_proctab/archive/refs/heads/master.zip -O pg_proctab-main.zip
unzip pg_proctab-main.zip
cd pg_proctab-master

docs.title: Step 3: Fix Makefile Wildcard Duplication (If applicable)
docs.text:
For pg_proctab specifically, apply a patch to prevent file duplication errors in the Makefile target:

[!NOTE] This patch is specific to pg_proctab to resolve a bug where the Makefile wildcard patterns match overlapping files. For other extensions, this step is not required and should be skipped.

sed -i 's|DATA = \$(wildcard sql/\*--\*.sql) sql/\$(EXTENSION)--\$(EXTVERSION).sql|DATA = \$(sort \$(wildcard sql/\*--\*.sql) sql/\$(EXTENSION)--\$(EXTVERSION).sql)|' Makefile

docs.title: Step 4: Build the Extension
docs.text:
Compile the extension by pointing PG_CONFIG explicitly to the PostgreSQL 16 executable: 

make USE_PGXS=1 PG_CONFIG=/usr/pgsql-16/bin/pg_config

docs.title: Step 5: Install the Compiled Extension
docs.text:
Install the resulting .so file, .control file, and .sql script files into the PostgreSQL 16 directories: 

sudo make install USE_PGXS=1 PG_CONFIG=/usr/pgsql-16/bin/pg_config

docs.title: output files will be:
docs.text:
/usr/pgsql-16/lib/pg_proctab.so

/usr/pgsql-16/share/extension/pg_proctab.control

/usr/pgsql-16/share/extension/pg_proctab--0.0.13.sql

/usr/pgsql-16/share/extension/pg_proctab--0.0.9--0.0.10.sql

/usr/pgsql-16/share/extension/pg_proctab--0.0.5--0.0.6.sql

docs.title: 4. Database Activation
docs.text: After installation, activate the extension within your PostgreSQL instance.

docs.title: Step 1: Log in and Run SQL Commands
docs.text:
Connect to the database server using psql (adjust port if running on a custom port like 5433): 

sudo -u postgres /usr/pgsql-16/bin/psql -p 5432 -d mydatabase -c "CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pg_proctab;"

docs.title: Step 2: Auto-Install in All Existing Databases
docs.text:
To enable the extension in all current user databases, run: 

sudo -u postgres /usr/pgsql-16/bin/psql -p 5432 -t -c "SELECT datname FROM pg_database WHERE datistemplate = false;" | while read dbname; do
    if [ -n "$dbname" ]; then
        echo "Activating in: $dbname"
        sudo -u postgres /usr/pgsql-16/bin/psql -p 5432 -d "$dbname" -c "CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pg_proctab;"
    fi
done

docs.title: Step 3: Enable in Default Template Database (for all future DBs)
docs.text: sudo -u postgres /usr/pgsql-16/bin/psql -p 5432 -d template1 -c "CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pg_proctab;"

docs.title: PostgreSQL 17 Extension Compile Guide for RHEL 8
docs.text: Target Environment: RHEL 8 / AlmaLinux 8 / CentOS 8 PostgreSQL Version: 17 Extension: pg_proctab (or similar extensions built from source)

docs.title: 1. Do I need to install it in every single database?
docs.text:
Yes. In PostgreSQL, extensions are installed on a strictly per-database basis. The extension's functions will only be queryable inside the specific databases where you have executed CREATE EXTENSION;.

Pro-Tip for Future Databases: If you want the extension to be automatically available in every brand new database you create in the future, you should install it into the template1 database. PostgreSQL uses template1 as the default blueprint for all new databases.

docs.title: 2. Portability & Compilation Environment Notes
docs.text:
[!IMPORTANT] OS & Architecture Dependency: Compiling extensions generates dynamic library files (.so binaries). These binaries are strictly compiled for the specific compiler version, OS kernel version, and CPU architecture of the host machine. Consequently, they are strictly OS-dependent. For example, you cannot copy a .so binary compiled on RHEL 8 to an instance running on Ubuntu or another incompatible OS.

[!TIP] Using a Development/Build Server: If you are compiling the extension on a Development/Build server to avoid installing compiler tools (like gcc, make, and development headers) on the live production server: 1. The Development/Build server must run the exact same OS distribution, version, architecture, and PostgreSQL version as the Production server. 2. Once successfully built, copy the compiled files from the Dev server to the Production server at the exact same paths: - Shared library file (.so): to /usr/pgsql-17/lib/ - Control (.control) and SQL (.sql) files: to /usr/pgsql-17/share/extension/

[!NOTE] Example Extension Only: The step-by-step commands below use the pg_proctab extension as a reference example. If you are building a different extension, you must substitute the download URLs, directory names, makefile patches (if any), SQL/extension names, and any extension-specific prerequisite packages/libraries with your own extension's source code and requirements.

docs.title: 3. End-to-End Implementation Steps
docs.text: Below is the master step-by-step guide to downloading, compiling, and deploying the extension from source on your production server.

docs.title: Step 1: Install Development Tools
docs.text:
Install the compiler tools and the specific PostgreSQL 17 development headers needed to build the extension. 

sudo dnf install -y gcc make postgresql17-devel unzip wget redhat-rpm-config

docs.title: Step 2: Download and Extract the Source Code
docs.text:
Download the code directly from the official repository and unzip it. 

cd /tmp
wget https://github.com/markwkm/pg_proctab/archive/refs/heads/master.zip -O pg_proctab-main.zip
unzip pg_proctab-main.zip
cd pg_proctab-master

docs.title: Step 3: Patch the Makefile Bug (If applicable)
docs.text:
Apply this quick patch to fix a known duplicate file bug in the extension's Makefile, ensuring it doesn't crash during the installation phase.

[!NOTE] This patch is specific to pg_proctab to resolve a bug where the Makefile wildcard patterns match overlapping files. For other extensions, this step is not required and should be skipped.

sed -i 's|DATA = \$(wildcard sql/\*--\*.sql) sql/\$(EXTENSION)--\$(EXTVERSION).sql|DATA = \$(sort \$(wildcard sql/\*--\*.sql) sql/\$(EXTENSION)--\$(EXTVERSION).sql)|' Makefile

docs.title: Step 4: Compile the Native Binary
docs.text:
Run the compilation process, explicitly telling it to use the PostgreSQL 17 configuration. This generates the .so binary file specifically for your OS and Postgres version. 

make USE_PGXS=1 PG_CONFIG=/usr/pgsql-17/bin/pg_config

docs.title: Step 5: Install the Extension Files
docs.text:
Copy the compiled .so library, .control, and .sql files into the protected PostgreSQL system folders. 

sudo make install USE_PGXS=1 PG_CONFIG=/usr/pgsql-17/bin/pg_config

docs.title: Step 6: Enable in Your Databases
docs.text:
Log into your PostgreSQL instance and enable it for your current databases. (Adjust the port -p 5433 if your database runs on the default 5432)

For all existing databases at once (Automated Script): If you have many databases, you can use this quick bash script to loop through all of them and install the extension automatically:

# Loop through all non-template databases and install the extension
sudo -u postgres /usr/pgsql-17/bin/psql -p 5433 -t -c "SELECT datname FROM pg_database WHERE datistemplate = false;" | while read dbname; do
    if [ -n "$dbname" ]; then
        echo "Installing in database: $dbname"
        sudo -u postgres /usr/pgsql-17/bin/psql -p 5433 -d "$dbname" -c "CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pg_proctab;"
    fi
done

For all future databases (Optional): If you want the extension to automatically exist in any new databases you create tomorrow, install it into the template1 database blueprint: 

sudo -u postgres /usr/pgsql-17/bin/psql -p 5433 -d template1 -c "CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pg_proctab;"

docs.title: PG LOAD ANALYSIS SETUP [PaaS]
docs.text:
PostgreSQL Load Analysis

Azure Database for PostgreSQL - Flexible Server

Implementation Steps · Schema Changes · Analysis Queries · Retention Lifecycle

Ginesys / Browntape Technologies | DBA Team | June 2026

This is the consolidated PaaS implementation document. It combines the original v2.1 implementation steps (Phase 1-2), the DB Head schema change request (Phase 3: cpu_ms_est, blk_read/write_time, query_id), and the new Phase 4 Retention Lifecycle (3-day rolling purge via pg_cron). PostgreSQL version: PG 17 (Azure Flexible Server). The collection job uses PG17 column names shared_blk_read_time / shared_blk_write_time from pg_stat_statements. Deploy in order: Phase 1 → Phase 2 → Phase 3 → Phase 4.

docs.title: 1.1 Verify pg_stat_statements is enabled
docs.text:
Run on each Flexible Server cluster before starting. If not enabled, add to postgresql.conf (server parameters) and reload.

-- Check if extension is loaded

SELECT name, setting FROM pg_settings WHERE name = 'shared_preload_libraries';

-- Check extension exists

SELECT * FROM pg_extension WHERE extname = 'pg_stat_statements';

-- If not present, add to server parameters in Azure Portal:

-- shared_preload_libraries = 'pg_stat_statements'

-- Then run: 

CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pg_stat_statements;

docs.title: 1.2 Create monitoring user
docs.text:
Dedicated read-only role - do not use a superuser account for collection.

CREATE ROLE pg_monitor_reader LOGIN PASSWORD 'set-a-strong-password';
```sql
GRANT pg_monitor TO pg_monitor_reader;
```sql
GRANT CONNECT ON DATABASE postgres TO pg_monitor_reader;
```sql
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA public TO pg_monitor_reader;
```sql
GRANT SELECT ON pg_stat_statements TO pg_monitor_reader;
```sql
GRANT SELECT ON pg_stat_activity TO pg_monitor_reader;
```sql
GRANT SELECT ON pg_stat_database TO pg_monitor_reader;
```sql
GRANT SELECT ON pg_locks TO pg_monitor_reader;

docs.title: 1.3 Create the monitoring schema and tables
docs.text:
Created in a separate monitoring database - not on the production databases being measured. These are the final table definitions including all DB Head columns added in Phase 3.

CREATE DATABASE pg_loadmon;
\\c pg_loadmon
```sql
CREATE SCHEMA monitoring;

-- Statement-level snapshots (every 1 min)

CREATE TABLE monitoring.stmt_snapshots (
id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
captured_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW(),
dbname TEXT,
application_name TEXT,
query_text TEXT, -- first 200 chars
calls BIGINT,
total_exec_time DOUBLE PRECISION,
rows BIGINT,
shared_blks_hit BIGINT,
shared_blks_read BIGINT,
query_id BIGINT, -- queryid from pg_stat_statements
temp_blks_written BIGINT,
wal_bytes BIGINT,
blk_read_time DOUBLE PRECISION, -- our column name; source on PG17: shared_blk_read_time
blk_write_time DOUBLE PRECISION, -- our column name; source on PG17: shared_blk_write_time
cpu_ms_est DOUBLE PRECISION -- total_exec_time - shared_blk_read_time - shared_blk_write_time
);
```sql
CREATE INDEX ON monitoring.stmt_snapshots (captured_at);
CREATE INDEX ON monitoring.stmt_snapshots (query_id);
-- Active session snapshots (every 30 sec)

CREATE TABLE monitoring.session_snapshots (
id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
captured_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW(),
pid INT,
dbname TEXT,
application_name TEXT,
state TEXT,
wait_event_type TEXT,
wait_event TEXT,
query_start TIMESTAMPTZ,
duration_secs DOUBLE PRECISION,
query_id BIGINT -- from pg_stat_activity (Phase 3)
);
```sql
CREATE INDEX ON monitoring.session_snapshots (captured_at);
CREATE INDEX ON monitoring.session_snapshots (query_id);
-- Lock wait snapshots (every 30 sec)

CREATE TABLE monitoring.lock_snapshots (
id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
captured_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW(),
waiting_pid INT,
waiting_app TEXT,
blocking_pid INT,
blocking_app TEXT,
lock_type TEXT,
relation TEXT,
wait_secs DOUBLE PRECISION
);
```sql
CREATE INDEX ON monitoring.lock_snapshots (captured_at);

-- Database-level snapshots (every 60 sec)

CREATE TABLE monitoring.db_snapshots (
id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
captured_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW(),
dbname TEXT,
numbackends INT,
xact_commit BIGINT,
xact_rollback BIGINT,
blks_hit BIGINT,
blks_read BIGINT,
tup_returned BIGINT,
tup_fetched BIGINT
);
```sql
CREATE INDEX ON monitoring.db_snapshots (captured_at, dbname);

-- Grant INSERT + SELECT on all tables to collection user:

GRANT INSERT, SELECT ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA monitoring TO pg_monitor_reader;
```sql
GRANT USAGE, UPDATE ON ALL SEQUENCES IN SCHEMA monitoring TO pg_monitor_reader;
_The table definitions above are the final combined schema (v2.1 base + Phase 3 additions). If you already created the tables from v2.1, use the ALTER TABLE statements in Phase 3 instead of recreating._

docs.title: Phase 2 - Monitoring Stack Deployment (pg_cron Jobs)
docs.text:
All collection runs inside pg_loadmon via pg_cron using cron.schedule_in_database(). Connect as superuser to pg_loadmon to register jobs. Collection queries run as the postgres user inside pg_cron workers.

These are the final job definitions including all Phase 3 columns. If you already have earlier jobs registered, skip to Phase 3 Section 3.1 to drop and recreate them.

docs.title: 2.1 Job 1 - Statement snapshots (every 1 minute)
docs.text:
SELECT cron.schedule_in_database(
'collect_stmts',

'*/1 * * * *',

$$

INSERT INTO monitoring.stmt_snapshots
(dbname, application_name, query_text, calls, total_exec_time,

rows, shared_blks_hit, shared_blks_read, query_id,

temp_blks_written, wal_bytes,

blk_read_time, blk_write_time, cpu_ms_est)

SELECT
d.datname,

COALESCE(sa.application_name, 'unknown') AS application_name,

s.query AS query_text,

s.calls, s.total_exec_time, s.rows,

s.shared_blks_hit, s.shared_blks_read, s.queryid,

s.temp_blks_written, s.wal_bytes,

s.shared_blk_read_time, -- PG17+ name

s.shared_blk_write_time, -- PG17+ name

s.total_exec_time - s.shared_blk_read_time - s.shared_blk_write_time

FROM pg_stat_statements s
JOIN pg_database d ON d.oid = s.dbid

LEFT JOIN pg_stat_activity sa ON sa.query_id = s.queryid

AND sa.usesysid = s.userid

AND sa.state = 'active';

$$,

'postgres'

);

docs.title: 2.2 Job 2 - Sessions + locks at :00 (every minute)
docs.text:
SELECT cron.schedule_in_database(
'collect_sessions_locks_00',

'* * * * *',

$$

INSERT INTO monitoring.session_snapshots
(pid, dbname, application_name, state, wait_event_type,

wait_event, query_start, duration_secs, query_id)

SELECT pid, datname, application_name, state,
wait_event_type, wait_event, query_start,

EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (NOW() - query_start)),

query_id

FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE state = 'active' AND pid <> pg_backend_pid();

INSERT INTO monitoring.lock_snapshots
(waiting_pid, waiting_app, blocking_pid, blocking_app,

lock_type, relation, wait_secs)

SELECT w.pid, w.application_name, b.pid, b.application_name,
lw.locktype, c.relname,

EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (NOW() - w.query_start))

FROM pg_stat_activity w
JOIN pg_locks lw ON lw.pid = w.pid AND NOT lw.granted

JOIN pg_locks lb ON lb.locktype = lw.locktype AND lb.granted

AND lb.relation IS NOT DISTINCT FROM lw.relation

JOIN pg_stat_activity b ON b.pid = lb.pid

LEFT JOIN pg_class c ON c.oid = lw.relation

WHERE w.wait_event_type = 'Lock';
$$,

'postgres'

);

docs.title: 2.3 Job 3 - Sessions + locks at :30 (offset by pg_sleep)
docs.text:
The leading SELECT pg_sleep(30) is plain SQL - do NOT use PERFORM here (pg_cron bodies are SQL, not PL/pgSQL). The pg_sleep appears as ~98% of pg_cron wall-clock in workload reports. It is harmless (zero CPU) but inflates pg_cron's wall-clock share - exclude it from load conclusions.

SELECT cron.schedule_in_database(
'collect_sessions_locks_30',

'* * * * *',

$$

SELECT pg_sleep(30);

INSERT INTO monitoring.session_snapshots
(pid, dbname, application_name, state, wait_event_type,

wait_event, query_start, duration_secs, query_id)

SELECT pid, datname, application_name, state,
wait_event_type, wait_event, query_start,

EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (NOW() - query_start)),

query_id

FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE state = 'active' AND pid <> pg_backend_pid();

INSERT INTO monitoring.lock_snapshots
(waiting_pid, waiting_app, blocking_pid, blocking_app,

lock_type, relation, wait_secs)

SELECT w.pid, w.application_name, b.pid, b.application_name,
lw.locktype, c.relname,

EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (NOW() - w.query_start))

FROM pg_stat_activity w
JOIN pg_locks lw ON lw.pid = w.pid AND NOT lw.granted

JOIN pg_locks lb ON lb.locktype = lw.locktype AND lb.granted

AND lb.relation IS NOT DISTINCT FROM lw.relation

JOIN pg_stat_activity b ON b.pid = lb.pid

LEFT JOIN pg_class c ON c.oid = lw.relation

WHERE w.wait_event_type = 'Lock';
$$,

'postgres'

);

docs.title: 2.4 Job 4 - Database stats (every 1 minute)
docs.text:
SELECT cron.schedule_in_database(
'collect_db_stats',

'* * * * *',

$$

INSERT INTO monitoring.db_snapshots
(dbname, numbackends, xact_commit, xact_rollback,

blks_hit, blks_read, tup_returned, tup_fetched)

SELECT datname, numbackends, xact_commit, xact_rollback,
blks_hit, blks_read, tup_returned, tup_fetched

FROM pg_stat_database
WHERE datname NOT IN ('template0', 'template1', 'postgres');
$$,

'postgres'

);

docs.title: 2.5 Verify all four jobs are registered
docs.text:
SELECT jobid, jobname, schedule, database, active
FROM cron.job
ORDER BY jobid;

docs.title: Phase 3 - Schema Changes (DB Head Request)
docs.text: Purpose: Two additive schema changes. Change 1 adds blk_read_time, blk_write_time, and derived cpu_ms_est to stmt_snapshots, giving an estimated CPU figure from pg_stat_statements alone. Change 2 adds query_id to session_snapshots so active sessions can be linked back to their statement. Both are additive - no existing columns change. Skip if you created tables using the Phase 1 definitions above (they already include these columns).

docs.title: 3.1 Prerequisites
docs.text:
Enable track_io_timing

blk_read_time and blk_write_time are ALWAYS ZERO unless track_io_timing is ON. Without this setting, cpu_ms_est equals total_exec_time, which is meaningless. Note: on PG 17 the source columns are named shared_blk_read_time / shared_blk_write_time in pg_stat_statements - the collection job uses these PG17 names.

SHOW track_io_timing; -- should return 'on'

-- If off, set in Azure Portal > Server Parameters:

-- track_io_timing = on

-- Then reload (no restart needed):

SELECT pg_reload_conf();
_Overhead: track_io_timing calls the OS clock on every block read/write. On Azure Flexible Server (modern Linux, tsc clock source) this overhead is negligible._

Verify compute_query_id

SHOW compute_query_id; -- should be 'on' or 'auto'

-- With pg_stat_statements already loaded, 'auto' is normally on.

-- If off: set compute_query_id = auto in Server Parameters and reload.

docs.title: 3.2 Change 1 - Add I/O timing and estimated CPU to stmt_snapshots
docs.text:
Run these ALTER statements on the existing table if upgrading from v2.1 base. If created fresh in Phase 1, these columns already exist.

ALTER TABLE monitoring.stmt_snapshots
ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS blk_read_time DOUBLE PRECISION, -- our column (source PG17: shared_blk_read_time)

ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS blk_write_time DOUBLE PRECISION, -- our column (source PG17: shared_blk_write_time)

ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS cpu_ms_est DOUBLE PRECISION; -- total_exec_time - shared_blk_read_time - shared_blk_write_time
-- cpu_ms_est formula (PG17): total_exec_time - shared_blk_read_time - shared_blk_write_time

-- Removes disk I/O wait. Does NOT remove lock/latch/sleep waits.

-- Label it as an estimate in reports. PG17 REQUIRED CHANGE: pg_stat_statements on PostgreSQL 17+ renamed blk_read_time → shared_blk_read_time and blk_write_time → shared_blk_write_time (and added local/temp_variants). The collection job above uses the PG17 names. Your monitoring.stmt_snapshots column names (blk_read_time, blk_write_time) are unchanged - only the source pg_stat_statements column names differ. On PG 16 reverse the names back. Verify your version's column names: SELECT column_name FROM information_schema.columns WHERE table_name='pg_stat_statements' AND column_name LIKE '%blk%time%';_

docs.title: 3.3 Change 2 - Add query_id to session_snapshots
docs.text:
ALTER TABLE monitoring.session_snapshots
ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS query_id BIGINT;
```sql
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS ix_session_snap_qid
ON monitoring.session_snapshots (query_id);

docs.title: 3.4 Drop and recreate pg_cron jobs
docs.text:
The two schema changes require the collection jobs to be updated. Drop existing jobs first, then recreate using the Phase 2 definitions (which already include all new columns).

-- Drop existing jobs:

SELECT cron.unschedule('collect_stmts');
```sql
SELECT cron.unschedule('collect_sessions_locks_00');
```sql
SELECT cron.unschedule('collect_sessions_locks_30');
```sql
SELECT cron.unschedule('collect_db_stats');

-- Verify cleared:

SELECT jobid, jobname, schedule, database, active FROM cron.job ORDER BY jobid;

-- Then recreate using the four job definitions in Phase 2 (Sections 2.1-2.4). Order of operations: (1) enable track_io_timing + verify compute_query_id, (2) run both ALTER TABLE statements, (3) drop and recreate jobs. If the columns do not exist when a job runs, the INSERT fails and that snapshot is lost.

docs.title: 3.5 Verification after collection
docs.text:
-- Change 1: timing populated (non-zero if track_io_timing=on)

SELECT query_id, blk_read_time, blk_write_time, cpu_ms_est
FROM monitoring.stmt_snapshots
WHERE captured_at >= NOW() - INTERVAL '10 minutes'
AND blk_read_time > 0 LIMIT 5;

-- Change 2: query_id populated in session_snapshots

SELECT pid, application_name, query_id
FROM monitoring.session_snapshots
WHERE captured_at >= NOW() - INTERVAL '10 minutes'
AND query_id IS NOT NULL LIMIT 5;

docs.title: 3.6 Analysis - Estimated CPU by application (DB Head rollup)
docs.text:
Ranks applications by estimated CPU instead of raw wall-clock. Built-in answer to I/O-bound vs CPU-bound question: 

SELECT
dbname,

ROUND((SUM(cpu_ms_est)/1000.0)::NUMERIC, 1) AS cpu_est_sec,

ROUND((100.0 * SUM(cpu_ms_est) /

NULLIF(SUM(SUM(cpu_ms_est)) OVER(), 0))::NUMERIC, 2) AS pct_cpu_est,

ROUND((SUM(total_exec_time)/1000.0)::NUMERIC, 1) AS wall_sec,

ROUND((SUM(blk_read_time + blk_write_time)/1000.0)::NUMERIC, 1) AS io_wait_sec,

ROUND((100.0 * SUM(blk_read_time + blk_write_time) /

NULLIF(SUM(total_exec_time), 0))::NUMERIC, 1) AS pct_io_wait

FROM monitoring.stmt_snapshots
WHERE captured_at >= NOW() - INTERVAL '24 hours'
GROUP BY dbname
ORDER BY cpu_est_sec DESC;

docs.title: 3.7 Analysis - Link active sessions to statement cost (query_id join)
docs.text:
Shows which query_ids were most often caught actively running, and what they cost: 

SELECT
ss.query_id,

COUNT(*) AS times_caught_active,

MAX(st.query_text) AS query_text,

ROUND((MAX(st.cpu_ms_est)/1000.0)::NUMERIC,1) AS cpu_est_sec,

ROUND((MAX(st.blk_read_time)/1000.0)::NUMERIC,1) AS io_read_sec

FROM monitoring.session_snapshots ss
LEFT JOIN LATERAL (
SELECT query_text, cpu_ms_est, blk_read_time
FROM monitoring.stmt_snapshots st
WHERE st.query_id = ss.query_id
ORDER BY st.captured_at DESC LIMIT 1
) st ON true
WHERE ss.captured_at >= NOW() - INTERVAL '24 hours'
AND ss.query_id IS NOT NULL

GROUP BY ss.query_id
ORDER BY times_caught_active DESC
LIMIT 30;

docs.title: 3.8 DB Head Attribution Rollup Query
docs.text:
Per-application breakdown of execution time, I/O, temp I/O, WAL writes, and buffer cache hit ratio: 

WITH ranked AS (
SELECT
application_name, query_id,

MAX(total_exec_time) AS latest_exec_ms,

MAX(calls) AS latest_calls,

MAX(rows) AS latest_rows,

MAX(shared_blks_read) AS latest_blks_read,

MAX(shared_blks_hit) AS latest_blks_hit,

MAX(temp_blks_written) AS latest_temp_blks,

MAX(wal_bytes) AS latest_wal_bytes,

COUNT(*) AS times_observed_active

FROM monitoring.stmt_snapshots
WHERE captured_at >= NOW() - INTERVAL '24 hours'
GROUP BY application_name, query_id
),

totals AS (

SELECT
application_name,

SUM(latest_exec_ms) AS grp_exec_ms,

SUM(latest_calls) AS grp_calls,

SUM(latest_rows) AS grp_rows,

SUM(latest_blks_read) AS grp_blks_read,

SUM(latest_blks_hit) AS grp_blks_hit,

SUM(latest_temp_blks) AS grp_temp_blks,

SUM(latest_wal_bytes) AS grp_wal_bytes,

SUM(times_observed_active) AS grp_active_observations

FROM ranked
GROUP BY application_name
)

SELECT
application_name,

grp_calls,

ROUND((grp_exec_ms / 1000.0)::NUMERIC, 1) AS total_exec_sec,

ROUND((100.0 * grp_exec_ms / SUM(grp_exec_ms) OVER())::NUMERIC, 2) AS pct_exec_time,

grp_rows,

grp_blks_read AS disk_reads,

ROUND((100.0 * grp_blks_read /

NULLIF(SUM(grp_blks_read) OVER(), 0))::NUMERIC, 2) AS pct_disk_reads,

ROUND((100.0 * grp_blks_hit /

NULLIF(grp_blks_read + grp_blks_hit, 0))::NUMERIC, 2) AS buffer_hit_pct,

grp_temp_blks AS temp_io_blks,

ROUND((grp_wal_bytes / 1024.0 / 1024.0)::NUMERIC, 2) AS wal_mb,

ROUND((100.0 * grp_wal_bytes /

NULLIF(SUM(grp_wal_bytes) OVER(), 0))::NUMERIC, 2) AS pct_wal_writes,

grp_active_observations

FROM totals
ORDER BY pct_exec_time DESC;

docs.title: Phase 4 - Retention Lifecycle (3-Day Rolling Window)
docs.text: All four monitoring tables grow continuously. Without a purge job the pg_loadmon database will exhaust its Azure disk allocation within days. The policy is: keep exactly 3 days of data, delete everything older. On Azure Flexible Server, retention is implemented as a daily pg_cron job - no shell scripts, no external schedulers.

docs.title: 4.1 Data Growth Estimates
docs.text:
Table Rows/day MB/day 3-day cap Collection frequency stmt_snapshots ~144,000 ~62 MB ~186 MB Every 1 min via pg_cron (1,440 snapshots × ~100 queries/min) session_snapshots ~57,600 ~11 MB ~33 MB Every 30 sec via pg_cron (active sessions only) lock_snapshots negligible <1 MB <3 MB Every 30 sec (rows only when lock waits exist) db_snapshots ~14,400 ~1 MB ~3 MB Every 60 sec (1,440 × ~10 databases) TOTAL (raw + index ~2×) ~216,000 ~75 MB ~225 MB Stable ceiling once purge job is running

session_snapshots and lock_snapshots only insert rows when sessions are active / when locks exist - so their actual volume is lower than the theoretical max shown above. stmt_snapshots is the dominant table on busy servers because it captures every tracked query shape every minute.

docs.title: 4.2 One-Time Permission Grant
docs.text:
The pg_monitor_reader role has INSERT and SELECT on all monitoring tables. DELETE must be added once before the purge job will succeed:

-- Run as superuser (postgres) once in pg_loadmon:

GRANT DELETE ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA monitoring TO pg_monitor_reader;
_Without this grant, the purge pg_cron job will fail with a permission denied error. The collection jobs will continue to run but the tables will keep growing._

docs.title: 4.3 Purge Job - pg_cron (runs daily at 02:00)
docs.text:
Register a single pg_cron job that deletes rows older than 3 days from all four tables, then issues VACUUM on each to reclaim pages. This runs inside PostgreSQL - no shell access needed on Azure Flexible Server.

SELECT cron.schedule_in_database(
'purge_monitoring_3day',

'18 31 * * *', -- daily at 02:00 (server local time)

$$

-- ── DELETE old rows (3-day retention) ────────────────────────────

DELETE FROM monitoring.stmt_snapshots
WHERE captured_at < NOW() - INTERVAL '3 days';

DELETE FROM monitoring.session_snapshots
WHERE captured_at < NOW() - INTERVAL '3 days';

DELETE FROM monitoring.lock_snapshots
WHERE captured_at < NOW() - INTERVAL '3 days';

DELETE FROM monitoring.db_snapshots
WHERE captured_at < NOW() - INTERVAL '3 days';
$$,

'postgres'

);

Why 02:00: after the nightly pg_basebackup backup window and before the morning OLTP peak. The purge deletes ~216,000 rows and VACUUMs four tables - at 02:00 this completes in seconds. Adjust the schedule if your backup window is different.

docs.title: 4.4 Important: VACUUM inside pg_cron on Flexible Server
docs.text:
Azure Flexible Server restricts VACUUM inside pg_cron on some versions. If the purge job fails with 'VACUUM cannot run inside a transaction block', replace the four VACUUM statements with a single call to autovacuum or remove them entirely. Autovacuum will handle the dead tuples on its next run. The DELETE rows are still removed; only the page reclamation is delayed.

Alternative if VACUUM fails inside pg_cron - register a separate job that calls VACUUM outside a transaction block:

-- Alternative: separate VACUUM job (runs right after purge at 02:05)

SELECT cron.schedule_in_database(
'vacuum_monitoring',

'31 18 * * *',

$$

VACUUM monitoring.stmt_snapshots;

VACUUM monitoring.session_snapshots;

VACUUM monitoring.lock_snapshots;

VACUUM monitoring.db_snapshots;
$$,

'pg_loadmon'

);

-- If VACUUM still fails, remove from purge job and rely on autovacuum.

-- Autovacuum fires automatically once dead tuple threshold is reached.

-- Check autovacuum activity: 

SELECT * FROM pg_stat_user_tables
WHERE schemaname = 'monitoring' ORDER BY n_dead_tup DESC;

docs.title: 4.5 Verify Purge Job is Registered
docs.text:
-- Confirm the job exists:

SELECT jobid, jobname, schedule, database, active
FROM cron.job
WHERE jobname = 'purge_monitoring_3day';

-- Check last run status (after first execution):

SELECT jobid, status, return_message, start_time, end_time
FROM cron.job_run_details
WHERE jobid = (SELECT jobid FROM cron.job WHERE jobname = 'purge_monitoring_3day')
ORDER BY start_time DESC LIMIT 5;

docs.title: 4.6 Verify Retention Is Working
docs.text:
Run after the first purge execution to confirm the window is correct and table sizes are stable:

-- Oldest row in each table (should be ~3 days ago):

SELECT 'stmt_snapshots' AS tbl, MIN(captured_at) AS oldest,
MAX(captured_at) AS newest, COUNT(*) AS rows
FROM monitoring.stmt_snapshots
UNION ALL
SELECT 'session_snapshots', MIN(captured_at), MAX(captured_at), COUNT(*)
FROM monitoring.session_snapshots
UNION ALL
SELECT 'lock_snapshots', MIN(captured_at), MAX(captured_at), COUNT(*)
FROM monitoring.lock_snapshots
UNION ALL
SELECT 'db_snapshots', MIN(captured_at), MAX(captured_at), COUNT(*)
FROM monitoring.db_snapshots
ORDER BY tbl;

-- Physical table sizes:

SELECT relname,
pg_size_pretty(pg_total_relation_size(oid)) AS total_size
FROM pg_class
WHERE relnamespace = (
SELECT oid FROM pg_namespace WHERE nspname = 'monitoring')
AND relkind = 'r'
ORDER BY pg_total_relation_size(oid) DESC;

Expected steady state: oldest row ~3 days ago for all tables, total size across all four tables ~200-300 MB. If total_size keeps growing day-over-day, the purge job is not running - check cron.job_run_details for errors and confirm the DELETE grant was applied.

docs.title: Deployment Order Summary
docs.text:
Follow this sequence exactly. Each phase depends on the previous.

Step Action Section Notes 1 Enable track_io_timing + verify compute_query_id Phase 3 § 3.1 Reload only, no restart. Must be done before ALTER TABLE. 2 Create pg_loadmon database + all four tables Phase 1 § 1.3 Use Phase 1 definitions (include all Phase 3 columns). Skip if upgrading - go to Step 3. 3 ALTER TABLE (upgrades only) Phase 3 § 3.2-3.3 Only needed if tables were created from v2.1 base. New installs skip this. 4 Grant DELETE to pg_monitor_reader Phase 4 § 4.2 One-time. Required for purge job. 5 Register collection jobs (Jobs 1-4) Phase 2 § 2.1-2.4 Or drop + recreate if upgrading from v2.1. 6 Register purge job Phase 4 § 4.3 Daily at 02:00.
